What to Expect: Sunrise over Bandarpoonch, Swargarohini and the Gangotri peaks The Doon valley on one side, the Yamuna valley on the other Breakfast at camp, then an easy 4 km, 1.5–2 hr walk back through the forest Drive from Cloud End through Mussoorie to Dehradun (35 km, ~2 hrs)
Return train or bus booked for the afternoon or evening Trek ends at Cloud End; drop at Dehradun by early afternoon How To Reach
By Air
By Train
By Bus
Nearest airport: Jolly Grant Airport (DED), Dehradun – about 25 km / 45–60 min from Dehradun city, with direct flights from Delhi and other metros. The cab to Cloud End leaves Dehradun Railway Station in the morning, so arrive the evening before and stay in Dehradun.
From Dehradun to Cloud End:
about 35 km via Mussoorie, roughly 2 hrs depending on traffic. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs, paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers. Your trek coordinator will confirm the cab fare. The cab leaves Dehradun Railway Station in the mo

itinerary.title: Manali to Gulaba and trek to Gulaba Meadows Camp
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Pickup: Beas Bridge, Manali, 10:00 AM | Drive: Manali → Gulaba (~22 km, ~1 hr) | Trek: ~4 km, 3–4 hrs | Terrain: steady climb through deodar, oak and maple forest to open meadows | Stay: Tents on the meadows above Gulaba
The group meets at Beas Bridge in Manali at 10:00 AM. From there you drive about 22 km up the Manali–Rohtang road, towards Rohtang Pass, to the small roadhead at Gulaba. The drive takes around an hour. At Gulaba there is a quick gear check and a briefing, and then the trek begins straight into the forest. Keep your water bottle and a light layer in your daypack, not in the main bag.
Today is short on distance but steady on the climb. The trail gains height through tall deodar, oak and maple, and it rarely eases off. Walk at a pace where you can still talk. If you cannot finish a sentence, slow down. In our experience the first day sets your rhythm for the whole trek, so it pays to start slower than feels necessary. Short, regular sips of water work better than long stops.
The forest looks different with the season. In the monsoon the floor is green and full of ferns and wild flowers. In late spring and autumn the light through the trees is sharp and clear. Within a couple of hours the forest opens into rolling meadows, and the peaks of the Pir Panjal start to appear above the trees. This is the first of the open views that stay with you for the rest of the trek.
Camp is pitched on the meadows above Gulaba, and the rest of the day is for recovery. Rest, drink water steadily and let your body begin to adjust to the altitude. In the evening there is a briefing, then dinner and your first night in the mountains. Nights on this trek drop to between -2 C and 4 C in late May and early October, and to 2–8 C in the monsoon months, so keep a warm layer close.
What to Expect: Short morning drive from Manali up the Manali–Rohtang road to Gulaba
Gear check and briefing at the Gulaba roadhead Steady ~4 km climb through deodar, oak and maple forest

itinerary.title: Gulaba Meadows to Rola Kholi
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: up to ~3,900 m (12,800 ft) | Distance: ~4 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Terrain: last of the tree line, then open alpine grassland, steady and in places steep | Stay: Tents at Rola Kholi
Today the trail leaves the forest behind. You climb through high meadows and the last of the tree line into open alpine grassland, the thatch this trek is known for. The distance is only about 4 km, but it takes 4–5 hours, because the gradient is steady and in places steep. Your trek leader keeps a slow, even pace with regular breaks. Take short steps on the steep parts and keep your breathing even. Stay with that pace, even if you feel strong. The altitude gained today matters more than the kilometres.
Drink 3 to 4 litres of water through the day. Good hydration is your best protection against altitude sickness, and in our experience it is the one habit that makes the biggest difference on this trek. Sip at every break rather than drinking a lot at once, and do not wait until you feel thirsty.
As you gain height, the view opens up across the Kullu valley. Hanuman Tibba and Deo Tibba rise across the valley, with the jagged line of the Seven Sisters beside them. From June to August these grassy slopes are covered in wild flowers. Turn around now and then at the breaks; much of the view is behind you as you climb. Stop for photographs at the breaks rather than on the steep sections.
Camp tonight is at Rola Kholi, at about 3,900 m (12,800 ft). It is a meadow beside a stream, and the base camp for Bhrigu Lake. After lunch you take a short walk higher up and back down again. This acclimatisation walk helps your body adjust before tomorrow, so join it even if you would rather rest. Then comes an early dinner and an early night. Before you sleep, lay out your warm layers, headlamp and water bottle for the early start. Tomorrow is the big day, and it starts before sunrise.
What to Expect: Climb out of the forest into open alpine grassland: ~4 km, 4–5 hrs Slow, even pace

itinerary.title: Rola Kholi to Bhrigu Lake and back to Rola Kholi
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: ~3,900 m → ~4,300 m (14,100 ft) → ~3,900 m | Distance: ~9 km round trip | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: steep grassy slopes, then loose rock and boulders above the tree line | Stay: Tents at Rola Kholi
The day starts early, with breakfast before sunrise. You leave camp early to reach the lake before the afternoon cloud comes in. Above Rola Kholi the trail climbs steep grassy slopes straight away, with no warm-up. Have your daypack ready with water, snacks, sunglasses and sunscreen before breakfast, so the group can leave on time. The morning is cold, so start in your warm layers and take them off as you heat up.
Higher up, the grass gives way to loose rock and boulders above the tree line. This is the hardest section of the trek. Take it slowly and use your trekking poles. Test each rock before you put your weight on it, keep your steps short and your breathing steady. There is no prize for reaching the lake first, and in our experience the trekkers who climb this section slowly arrive at the top in better shape.
Then the ridge flattens and Bhrigu Lake appears. It sits at about 4,300 m (14,100 ft): a small, deep glacial lake, turquoise or deep blue depending on the season. In late spring, snow lingers on its banks. The peaks of the Pir Panjal stand close around it. Local legend says the sage Maharishi Bhrigu meditated here, and villagers in the Kullu valley still treat the lake as sacred. Please do not throw anything into the water. The sun is strong at this height, even when the air feels cool, so wear sunglasses and sunscreen.
After time at the lake for photographs and rest, you walk back down the same way to Rola Kholi. Go carefully on the boulder section and keep using your poles. At camp a well-earned hot meal is waiting, followed by a celebration. Drink plenty of water once you are back. You have reached the high point of the trek, and you sleep at Rola Kholi again tonight.
What to Expect: Breakfast before sunrise and an early start to

itinerary.title: Rola Kholi to Gulaba and drive to Manali
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: ~3,900 m (12,800 ft) → Gulaba roadhead | Distance: ~8 km descent | Duration: 4–5 hrs trek + ~1 hr drive | Terrain: meadows, then forest | Stay: Not included (trek ends in Manali)
Your last morning at Rola Kholi starts with breakfast. Then you retrace the route down through the meadows and back into the forest, about 8 km and 4–5 hours on foot. With lighter packs and legs that are now used to the trail, the descent goes quickly. Take a last long look across the Kullu valley as you drop.
Downhill is hard on the knees, especially on the steeper forest sections. Shorten your poles slightly, take small steps and keep your speed under control. Let the poles take some of your weight on each step, and stop for water now and then.
The trek ends at the roadhead at Gulaba, where shared cabs, paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers, take you back to Manali in around an hour. You should be in town by early afternoon, in time for a hot shower and a walk around Old Manali. Breakfast is the last meal included, and your stay in Manali is not part of the trek.
What to Expect: Breakfast at Rola Kholi, then an ~8 km descent (4–5 hrs)
Meadows and forest on the way down, with last views of the Kullu valley Shorter poles and small steps to save your knees Drive from Gulaba to Manali, around 1 hr Back in Manali by early afternoon Trek ends at Gulaba; drop at Manali
How To Reach
By Air
By Train
By Bus
Nearest airport: Bhuntar Airport (Kullu–Manali, KUU), about 50 km / 1.5–2 hrs from Manali by taxi, with flights from Delhi. Flights are limited and weather-dependent, so plan to reach Manali the day before the trek starts.
From Manali to Gulaba: Day 1 begins with a 22 km, about 1 hr drive from Manali to Gulaba, then a 4 km (3–4 hr) walk to the Gulaba meadows camp. The shared taxi is paid by the trekkers, so carry cash from Manali. The pickup is at Beas Bridge, Manali at 10:00 AM on Day 1.
Return: On Day 4 you walk 8 km (4–5 hrs) down from Rola Kholi to Gul

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Binsar Sanctuary, Trek to Dhaulchina
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Kathgodam → Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary (130 km, about 5 hrs) | Trek: Binsar → Dhaulchina | Distance: 7 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Altitude: 2,250 m → 1,860 m We meet at Kathgodam Railway Station at 06:00 AM, in time for the overnight trains from Delhi. The shared cab climbs out of the plains past Bhimtal and on along the Kosi valley towards Almora, then turns north into the hills. It is a drive of about 130 km and 5 hours, with a breakfast stop on the way. Past Almora the road enters the Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary and winds up through thick forest.
We start walking at about 2,250 m (7,382 ft), inside the sanctuary. After a briefing, pulse and oxygen checks and a short stretch, the trail sets off through old oak and rhododendron forest, with moss and ferns on the trunks and dry leaves underfoot. The path descends gently most of the way, so the walking is easy, and there is plenty of time to stop and look around.
This is the richest stretch of the trek for wildlife and birds. Walk quietly and listen for the sharp bark of a barking deer, or watch the open slopes for goral. Where the trees open up, the first views of the snow peaks appear to the north. Your trek leader will point out the peaks and help you spot birds; keep a packed lunch and water handy for a break in a clearing along the way.
Lower down, the forest gives way to fields and the first village houses, and after about 7 km and 3–4 hours you reach Dhaulchina at 1,860 m (6,102 ft). The night is spent in a simple guesthouse or homestay in the village. Evening tea, a walk to watch the sunset over the hills and an early, hot dinner round off the day.
What to Expect: 06:00 AM pickup at Kathgodam Railway Station
Scenic 5-hour drive via the Kosi valley and Almora
A gentle forest descent through the Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary
Chances to see barking deer, goral and Himalayan birds First views of the snow peaks of Kumaon
Overnight: guesthouse or homestay at Dhaulchina

itinerary.title: Dhaulchina to Jageshwar via Vriddha Jageshwar, Drive to Kathgodam
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Trek: Dhaulchina → Vriddha Jageshwar → Jageshwar | Distance: 13 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Altitude: 1,860 m → 2,250 m → 1,870 m | Drive: Jageshwar → Kathgodam (about 125 km, 5 hrs)
Day 2 starts early, with breakfast at 06:30 AM and boots on by 07:30 AM, as there is a long walk and a long drive ahead. From Dhaulchina the trail climbs gradually through mixed forest of oak, pine and rhododendron, passing small hamlets and terraced fields where villagers are already at work. The gradient is gentle but steady; settle into a comfortable rhythm and take short breaks.
After about 3 hours you reach Vriddha Jageshwar at about 2,250 m (7,382 ft), a small, quiet shrine on the high ground above Jageshwar. Its name means old Jageshwar', and local belief holds that it predates the temples in the valley. On a clear day this is the main viewpoint of the trek, with Trishul, Nanda Devi and the peaks of Kumaon spread across the northern horizon. We stop here for a packed lunch.
From Vriddha Jageshwar the trail descends gradually for the rest of the day, first through open forest and then into tall deodar, the tree most closely linked with the Jageshwar valley. The path can be loose and dusty in dry months and frosty in winter, so trekking poles are useful. Your trek leader keeps the group together on the descent.
In the early afternoon the trees part and the temples of Jageshwar appear below, more than 125 stone shrines dedicated to Shiva beside the Jata Ganga stream. Take time to walk among them before the trek ends. From Jageshwar the shared cab drives back via Almora to Kathgodam, about 125 km and 5 hours, reaching the station between 06:30 PM and 07:30 PM depending on traffic and weather.
What to Expect: An early start and a gradual climb through village and forest Himalayan views from Vriddha Jageshwar at about 2,250 m (7,382 ft)
Long, gentle descent through deodar forest The ancient stone temples of Jageshwar beside the Jata Ganga
Evening drive back to Kathgodam, ar

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Lohajung
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Rishikesh → Lohajung | Distance: ~250 km | Duration: 8–10 hrs | Altitude: 340 m (Rishikesh) → 2,316 m (Lohajung)
Day 1 is an approach day, a long but scenically rewarding drive from the pilgrimage city of Rishikesh into the Garhwal interior, ending at Lohajung (2,316 m), the gateway village for the Brahmatal trek. The route follows NH7 and the state highways through the Alaknanda Valley, passing the Devprayag Sangam, where the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers meet to form the Ganga proper, a confluence of sacred geography that is worth the brief roadside stop. Above Rudraprayag, the valley narrows and the river runs faster below the road. Above Karnaprayag, the final hour of the drive climbs through progressively denser forest to Lohajung.
Lohajung in winter is a different village from its summer self. The surrounding forest carries the first snow on its upper edges in November, and by January the hillsides above the village are white. On clear mornings, Trishul (7,120 m) is visible above the forest ridgeline to the northeast, a distant white summit that is the first visual confirmation of where the next five days are taking you. The village is small, quiet, and genuinely connected to the mountain life of the Garhwal Chamoli district rather than to the trekking economy in any commodified way.
The evening in Lohajung is for rest, gear check, and the trek briefing. Trekkaro's health baseline SpO₂, pulse, and blood pressure for every trekker is recorded here at 2,316 m as the individual reference point for all subsequent daily readings on the route. The trek briefing covers the full six-day itinerary, the specific preparation required for winter snow trekking, the layering protocol for the temperature range ahead, and the AMS awareness relevant to the altitudes of Days 3 and 4. Sleep early and well.
What to Expect: Drive Rishikesh to Lohajung – ~250 km, 8–10 hrs via Devprayag, Rudraprayag, and Karnaprayag
Devprayag Sangam: confluence of Bhagirathi

itinerary.title: Lohajung to Bekaltal
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,316 m (Lohajung) → 2,798 m / 9,180 ft (Bekaltal) | Distance: ~6 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Terrain: Snow-covered forest trail, gradual climb through oak and rhododendron Day 2 is when Brahmatal begins to show you what it is. The trail from Lohajung enters the oak and rhododendron forest almost immediately and climbs steadily through a landscape that is, in winter, completely unlike anything on the summer trekking circuit. The trees are leafless and bare, their black branches coated in white frost, reaching upward against a sky that in the Garhwal winter is a blue of improbable intensity. The snow on the forest floor deepens progressively with altitude: at Lohajung, a few inches; by the time the trail reaches 2,800 m, knee-deep in places; by 3,000 m, the forest is buried to the waist in compressed snowpack that the oaks are growing through as though reclaiming the landscape from below.
The silence in the snow forest is a quality that most trekkers have not previously encountered. The snowpack absorbs sound in a way that the bare summer trail does not. Footsteps are muffled. The wind, which in summer rustles the oak canopy audibly, is reduced to a distant whisper above the snow-laden branches. The occasional crack of a snow-laden branch releasing its load, the distant sound of a bird, and the rhythmic crunch of boots on packed snow are the complete acoustic world of the Brahmatal forest in January. Many trekkers describe this section of the route as the most affecting they have encountered, not because of its visual scale, but because of its quality of deep, absolute quiet.
Bekaltal Lake, close to the camp at about 2,798 m (9,180 ft), is the first of the two lakes that give the Brahmatal route its character. In winter, the lake surface is frozen solid, a flat, white plane surrounded by snow-covered banks and the bare winter forest, with the sky and the occasional glimpse of a distant peak reflected in the ice at the margins where the surface c

itinerary.title: Bekaltal to Brahmatal Lake
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,798 m / 9,180 ft (Bekaltal) → Jhandi Top (~3,600 m) → Brahmatal Base Camp (3,106 m / 10,190 ft) | Distance: ~7 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: Steep snow ascent to Jhandi Top ridge, open ridge walk, descent to Brahmatal Lake basin Day 3 is the route's most visually dramatic day before the summit push and the day that earns its place at the centre of the itinerary through a combination of effort, exposure, and reward that the approach days cannot yet provide. The trail from Bekaltal climbs steeply through the upper forest before breaking above the treeline onto the Jhandi Top ridge at approximately 3,600 m. This ascent is the steepest section of the entire Brahmatal route, requiring microspikes from the Bekaltal camp upward and deliberate, measured movement on the compacted snow slope that leads to the ridge.
Jhandi Top is a snow ridge at approximately 3,600 m that serves as the viewpoint threshold between the enclosed forest terrain of the approach and the high mountain landscape ahead. When the ridge opens, it opens completely. To the north and northeast: Trishul (7,120 m) and Trishul East in full profile, the triple-peaked massif that dominates the western rim of the Nanda Devi Sanctuary, its upper snowfields brilliant white against the winter sky. Nanda Ghunti (6,309 m) sits immediately to its right, a sharper and more compact peak whose south face catches the morning sun in a composition that photographers consistently find impossible to adequately capture. To the north: Mt Kamet (7,756 m) on clear days, the second highest peak in Uttarakhand, as a massive white wall at the back of the range. Hathi Ghoda Parvat and the broader Garhwal Himalayan ridge extend across the entire northern horizon.
Most trekkers spend longer on Jhandi Top than the schedule strictly allows. The view from this ridge is the first unobstructed, high-altitude panorama of the trek, and it arrives after two days of forest walking in which the mountains were glimp

itinerary.title: Brahmatal Base Camp to Brahmatal Top & Return
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,106 m / 10,190 ft (Base Camp) → 3,734 m / 12,250 ft (Brahmatal Top) → return to Base Camp | Distance: ~6 km round trip | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: Steep snow ascent to the summit ridge, open ridge walk, return by the same route Day 4 is the summit day, a dedicated, focused push from the Brahmatal Base Camp to the top and back, with no other objective competing for the day's time or energy. Departure is at 5:30 AM, in the dark and in the cold that at this hour in January can be -15 C. Headlamps cut through the pre-dawn air as the group moves upward from the camp. The early departure is not ceremonial: the snow on the summit approach is at its firmest and most stable in the cold morning hours, and the Garhwal winter sky is at its clearest before the day's temperature inversion sometimes introduces a thin haze above the lower valleys.
The ascent from Base Camp to Brahmatal Top gains approximately 630 m across the upper snowfield and the final summit ridge. Microspikes are worn from the first step out of camp. The snow slope above the lake is steep but consistent, a sustained uphill push on compacted winter snow that requires deliberate, rhythmic movement and steady breathing. The trek leader sets the pace at a level that keeps every trekker moving continuously, because stopping in -15 C air without the thermal generation of movement means a rapid loss of core warmth that is difficult to reverse without physical activity. The group moves together, at a measured pace, in the pre-dawn quiet of the Garhwal winter.
As the summit ridge approaches and the terrain levels, the view begins to open. The forest and the lake are left below. The ridgeline ahead carries nothing but snow and sky. And then Brahmatal Top at 3,734 m (12,250 ft) delivers its complete panorama simultaneously, a 270-degree sweep of the Garhwal Himalayan range in winter clarity that is, for most trekkers, the finest summit view they have encountered at moderate grade anywhere in

itinerary.title: Brahmatal Base Camp to Lohajung
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,106 m / 10,190 ft (Base Camp) → Jhandi Top (~3,600 m) → Bekaltal (2,798 m) → Lohajung (2,316 m) | Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 7–8 hrs | Terrain: Ascent to Jhandi Top, descent through Bekaltal and snow forest to Lohajung
Day 5 is the longest trekking day of the route: a full descent from the Brahmatal Base Camp back to Lohajung, covering approximately 10 km across 7 to 8 hours. The route re-crosses Jhandi Top before descending through the Bekaltal basin and the snow forest to Lohajung. It is a demanding day, not in the sense of altitude gain, but in the sustained effort required to descend 790 m of mountain terrain in winter snow conditions while the body is carrying the accumulated fatigue of four consecutive high-altitude days.
The morning departure from Base Camp is early, with the Brahmatal Lake visible one final time in the dawn light before the group moves upward toward Jhandi Top for the return crossing. Jhandi Top on the return has a different character from Day 3. Then, the ridge opening was a revelation, the first unobstructed view of the Garhwal range arriving after two days of enclosed forest. Now, the same view is received as a farewell: Trishul and Nanda Ghunti in the morning light, with the knowledge that the summit above them has been reached and that the Brahmatal Base Camp where you slept two nights will not be seen again on this journey. Most trekkers spend a few minutes on the ridge on the return that the forward movement of Day 3 did not allow.
The descent from Jhandi Top through Bekaltal and down through the snow forest to Lohajung covers the same terrain as the approach in reverse. The snow forest, which on Day 2 was an arrival into an unfamiliar world, is received on Day 5 as familiar terrain being departed. The lake at Bekaltal, frozen then, is still frozen now. The silence of the forest is the same silence. But the body walking through it carries a summit, a panorama, and two nights at 3,106 m that the body ascend

itinerary.title: Drive from Lohajung to Rishikesh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Lohajung (2,316 m) → Karnaprayag → Rudraprayag → Devprayag → Rishikesh | Distance: ~250 km | Duration: 8–10 hrs The final morning in Lohajung has a particular quality. The Trishul summit visible above the forest ridgeline on clear mornings, the same peak whose distant white profile was the first visual confirmation of the trek's destination on Day 1, is now a peak you have seen in full, from a high viewpoint, in the winter Himalayan clarity that is at its sharpest between December and February. What was a distant aspiration on the approach is now a peak, you know.
The drive from Lohajung to Rishikesh retraces the approach road in reverse: back down through the Garhwal interior, through Karnaprayag, past the Rudraprayag confluence, past the Devprayag sangam where the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet in their most visually dramatic form, and then back to the broader, warmer, louder landscape of the Rishikesh valley. The 8- to 10-hour drive is long but covers scenery that is, in its own way, as significant as the trek itself: the river gorges of the Alaknanda, the terraced Garhwal hillsides, and the progressively widening valley as altitude decreases and the plains begin to reassert themselves at the lower end of the Himalayan range.
The cab is expected at Tapovan by 6:00 PM, so trekkers with onward connections can take a late-night train from Haridwar the same day, but should book flights from Dehradun for the next day. For those with more time, a night in Rishikesh at the ghats, in the ashrams, or simply at a restaurant that serves hot food is a transition from the Brahmatal winter world to the normal world that the experience deserves.
What to Expect: Drive Lohajung to Rishikesh – ~250 km, 8–10 hrs via Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag, and Devprayag
Devprayag Sangam: the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda confluence – the birth of the Ganga proper Alaknanda Valley: the same gorge road in reverse, seen now with five days of winter above it Onward connections: a late

itinerary.title: Arrival in Leh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Arrival: Leh by flight | Altitude: 3,500 m (11,483 ft) | Briefing: 12:00 noon (mandatory) | Stay: Centrally heated hotel (twin or triple sharing)
The Chadar Trek begins with a flight into Leh. Just before touchdown the approach gives you aerial views of the snow-covered Himalaya and the rugged Ladakhi landscape. Leh sits at 3,500 m (11,483 ft), and the cold, thin air meets you the moment you step out. Keep your woollen cap and gloves handy.
Check in to the centrally heated hotel; rooms have attached washrooms and hot water in buckets. At 12:00 noon the trek leader holds the mandatory orientation briefing on essential instructions, safety guidelines and acclimatisation. Bring your ID proof and 2 photographs; foreign nationals must carry their passport and visa. Keep your boarding pass as well, because it is required for the trek permission.
After the briefing, rest indoors and let your body adjust. Avoid high passes and any physical activity today. Smoking and alcohol are strictly prohibited. Leh has the last reliable ATM and mobile network, and only postpaid SIMs work here.
What to Expect: Aerial views of the snow-covered Himalaya on the flight into Leh
Mandatory orientation briefing at 12:00 noon Documents: ID proof and 2 photographs (passport and visa for foreign nationals); keep your boarding pass Rest indoors – no high passes, no exertion, no smoking or alcohol Last ATM and last mobile network (postpaid SIMs only) in Leh
Overnight: Centrally heated hotel in Leh (3,500 m / 11,483 ft)

itinerary.title: Acclimatisation Day in Leh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Rest day: Leh | Altitude: 3,500 m (11,483 ft) | Activity: short sightseeing tour (Hall of Fame, Shey Monastery, Thiksey Monastery) | Stay: Centrally heated hotel (twin or triple sharing)
Under the current regulations for the Chadar Trek, every trekker must spend at least two days in Leh before starting the trek. This is not a formality. Rest and gradual adaptation at 3,500 m reduce the risk of Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) before you head out onto the frozen Zanskar, where nights fall far below freezing.
The day is easy by design. A short sightseeing tour, included in the trek, takes you to the Hall of Fame, Shey Monastery and the Thiksey Monastery. These places show the culture and history of Ladakh and keep the day light without tiring you out. Walk slowly between stops and drink water regularly.
The trek leaders also hold an orientation session for the Chadar preparation. Avoid very high passes and regions during acclimatisation, and remember that smoking and alcohol remain strictly prohibited. You stay in the same centrally heated hotel, with attached washrooms and hot water.
What to Expect: Mandatory acclimatisation in Leh to reduce the risk of AMS
Short sightseeing tour: Hall of Fame, Shey Monastery and Thiksey Monastery
Orientation session by the trek leaders for Chadar preparation No high passes, no alcohol, no smoking Mobile network (postpaid only) and ATM still available in Leh
Overnight: Centrally heated hotel in Leh (3,500 m / 11,483 ft)

itinerary.title: Medical Test Day in Leh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Medical check: Government Medical Camp, Leh | Altitude: 3,500 m (11,483 ft) | Tests: height, weight, blood pressure, oxygen level | Afternoon: insurance formalities | Stay: Centrally heated hotel (twin or triple sharing)
Today decides whether you walk on the Chadar. Start early and head straight to the Government Medical Camp for the mandatory health check: height, weight, blood pressure and oxygen level. Because of the heavy tourist rush the process can take 3 to 4 hours, so be on time and carry water and a snack for the queue.
The results of the check-up determine whether you are medically fit to proceed with the trek. In the afternoon you complete the insurance formalities; high-altitude risk insurance is mandatory under ALTOA guidelines. The pre-medical check-up fee, rescue fees, wildlife and environmental charges, the ALTOA NOC and entry fees are paid directly to the authorities on the spot.
Once the formalities are done, the evening is free. Stroll around Leh at an easy pace, enjoy the crisp mountain air and then get a good night in the heated hotel. Tomorrow you leave for the river.
What to Expect: Early start for the mandatory check at the Government Medical Camp
Tests: height, weight, blood pressure and oxygen level; a 3–4 hour wait is possible Insurance formalities in the afternoon (high-altitude risk insurance is mandatory)
Medical, permit and NOC fees paid directly to the authorities Free evening to walk around Leh
Overnight: Centrally heated hotel in Leh (3,500 m / 11,483 ft)

itinerary.title: Leh to Shingra Koma, Trek to Tsomo Paldar
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Leh → Shingra Koma (75 km, 3–4 hrs) | Altitude: 3,150 m → 3,200 m (10,500 ft) | Distance: 3 km | Duration: 2 hrs | Terrain: frozen Zanskar River (the Chadar), in gumboots | Stay: Tents at Tsomo Paldar
After breakfast at the hotel you drive 75 km from Leh to Shingra Koma, about 3 to 4 hours. The road passes Gurudwara Pathar Sahib (3,500 m), Magnetic Hill (3,350 m) and the confluence of the Indus and the Zanskar (3,100 m). Look out for the meeting of the two rivers; it is your first sight of the Zanskar you will be walking on.
Shingra Koma sits at a U-bend in the Zanskar River, among dramatic cliffs, at 3,150 m (10,335 ft). This is where you step onto the Chadar for the first time. Chadar means blanket, the name for the sheet of ice that covers the river in winter. Gumboots are mandatory, and walking on ice in them takes practice.
The first walk is short, 3 km in about 2 hours, and its real purpose is to teach you the ice. Expect slips and slow progress at first. Keep your knees soft, take short steps and keep your weight over your feet. With patience you learn to tell fragile ice from firm. Follow the line your guide takes and step where the people ahead have stepped. The rock formations and patterns in the ice around you make the slow pace easy to accept.
A hot lunch is served on the way, before you reach Tsomo Paldar at 3,200 m (10,500 ft), your first camp on the river. Tents are on triple sharing, with towering cliffs around you and the frozen Zanskar beside camp. Night temperatures on the Chadar range from -15 to -30 C, so change into warm, dry layers as soon as you stop. Trekkaro provides sub-zero sleeping bags for the camping nights.
What to Expect: 75 km drive via Pathar Sahib, Magnetic Hill and the Indus–Zanskar confluence First steps on the Chadar at Shingra Koma (3,150 m / 10,335 ft), at a U-bend of the Zanskar
Gumboots mandatory – learn to tell fragile ice from firm Short 3 km, 2-hour walk with a hot lunch on the way Riverside camp be

itinerary.title: Tsomo Paldar to Tibb Cave
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,200 m → 3,350 m (10,991 ft) | Distance: 14 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: frozen river, gradual gain with no steep climbs | Stay: Tents at Tibb Cave
Today is long but gentle. You cover 14 km on the frozen Zanskar, and the trail rises only gradually, from 10,500 ft to 10,991 ft, with no steep climbs. The challenge is time on the ice. Six to seven hours in gumboots on slippery surfaces is tiring in its own way, so keep your pace even and take short pauses rather than long stops in the cold.
This is one of the most scenic stretches of the Chadar Trek. You walk beside the Zanskar, where emerald-green water shimmers against the frozen landscape. Frozen waterfalls hang on the cliffs along the way, their sources unknown and wrapped in local legends. One waterfall here never freezes, even in sub-zero temperatures, and it remains a mystery to trekkers and locals alike.
Sunlight reaches the river only between 9 and 10 AM on this stretch, so the hour of sun is something to look forward to. Along the trail you also pass small caves where local porters traditionally rest, a glimpse into their rugged way of life. Keep reading the ice the way you learnt yesterday and stay on the line your guide picks.
A hot lunch is served on the way. The day ends at the Tibb Cave campsite at 3,350 m, where you settle into triple-sharing tents beside the frozen river. Change out of damp socks as soon as you reach camp and keep your gloves dry for the evening.
What to Expect: Long 14 km day with gradual gain and no steep climbs Emerald-green Zanskar water against the white ice Frozen waterfalls, and one waterfall that never freezes Sunlight on the river only between 9 and 10 AM
Small caves used by local porters as rest stops; hot lunch on the way Overnight: Tents at Tibb Cave (3,350 m / 10,991 ft)

itinerary.title: Tibb Cave to Nerak
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,350 m → 3,400 m (11,155 ft) | Distance: 13 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: frozen river through deep gorges and between tall cliffs | Stay: Tents at Nerak
This is the most awaited day of the Chadar Trek. Over 13 km you walk the frozen Zanskar through deep gorges and between tall cliffs, in a landscape that feels otherworldly. The ice changes with the temperature, so keep reading the surface the way you have learnt over the last two days and stay on the line your guide picks.
Midway you stop for a hot lunch, then continue towards Nerak. The highlight of the trek waits here: the frozen Nerak waterfall, a towering cascade frozen solid into a sculpture of ice. It is the most iconic sight on the Chadar and draws trekkers from around the world. Give yourself time with it before you move on to camp.
Nerak is the first village of the Zanskar region, and the campsite gives you a glimpse of life in this remote, frozen valley. If time permits, a short visit to Nerak village can be arranged. In winter the frozen river is the only way in and out of these villages, which helps you understand what the Chadar means to the people who live here.
Be ready for the cold. Nerak is the coldest campsite of the trek, and night temperatures can drop to -30 C. Proper layering, insulated gloves, a woollen cap and thermals are essential tonight. Eat a full meal, change into dry layers and get into your sub-zero sleeping bag early.
What to Expect: 13 km through deep gorges and tall cliffs on the frozen Zanskar
Hot lunch break midway The frozen Nerak waterfall, the most iconic sight of the trek Nerak, the first village of Zanskar – short village visit if time permits Coldest campsite of the trek, with nights down to -30 C
Overnight: Tents at Nerak (3,400 m / 11,155 ft)

itinerary.title: Nerak to Tibb Cave
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,400 m → 3,350 m (10,991 ft) | Distance: 13 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: frozen river, return leg on changing ice | Stay: Tents at Tibb Cave
Today you turn back down the river and begin the return leg. Do not expect a repeat of the walk up. The Chadar changes all the time: ice you crossed yesterday may have cracked or vanished, and new layers form overnight. The route can look completely different, and that constant change is both the challenge and the charm of this trek.
The scenery is just as striking on the way back. Snow-covered cliffs rise on both sides, emerald-green water flows beneath the ice and frozen waterfalls hang like glass sculptures. Along the way you say goodbye to the locals and porters you have met in the valley, a warm farewell to the people of the Zanskar.
A hot lunch break en route gives you warmth and energy in the freezing conditions. You will be tired by now, and tired legs are less careful. Keep the same discipline you had on the way up: short steps, a steady pace and your eyes on the ice. Treat any section that looks different with care, and follow your guide's line.
By evening you reach Tibb Cave at 3,350 m for your final night in tents. Take a few minutes outside before bed. The valley is silent, the stars are bright on a clear night, and you can look back on days of walking one of the most iconic trails in the Himalaya.
What to Expect: Return leg on a Chadar that has changed since the way up Snow-covered cliffs, emerald water beneath the ice and frozen waterfalls Farewell to locals and porters along the way Hot lunch break en route Final night in tents on the Zanskar
Overnight: Tents at Tibb Cave (3,350 m / 10,991 ft)

itinerary.title: Tibb Cave to Shingra Koma, Drive to Leh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,350 m → 3,150 m (10,335 ft) | Distance: 17 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: frozen river | Drive: Shingra Koma → Leh (75 km, 3–4 hrs) | Stay: Centrally heated hotel in Leh
The final day on the ice starts early. The trail may feel familiar, but it is never quite the same. The ice sheet shifts with every change in temperature, so sections that were firm may now be fragile, and rocks and the emerald water of the Zanskar show up in new forms. At 17 km this is the longest day of the trek, so keep your focus to the last step.
The walk back to Shingra Koma is your last chance to take in the frozen wilderness, admire the sheer cliffs and the patterns in the ice, and take a few final photographs. Even on a return journey, the landscape looks entirely different from the way up. A hot lunch is served en route, a welcome break from the biting cold.
At Shingra Koma vehicles wait for the drive of about 75 km back to Leh. The road retraces the route through the confluence of the Zanskar and the Indus, Magnetic Hill and Gurudwara Pathar Sahib. Sit back and let your legs rest.
By evening you are back at the hotel in Leh, centrally heated and with running hot water. After days in tents and nights far below freezing, a hot shower and a warm room feel like pure luxury. It is the right place to rest, celebrate and look back on your days on the frozen Zanskar.
What to Expect: Early start for the longest day on the ice: 17 km A Chadar that keeps changing with the temperature Hot lunch on the way to Shingra Koma
75 km drive to Leh via the Indus–Zanskar confluence and Magnetic Hill
Centrally heated hotel with running hot water Overnight: Hotel in Leh (3,500 m / 11,483 ft)

itinerary.title: Departure from Leh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Departure: Leh | Hotel check-out: 10:00 AM | Airport cab: not included; we help you book one Your Chadar Trek ends in Leh today. Hotel check-out is at 10:00 AM, so pack the night before and leave yourself an unhurried morning. Airport transfers are not included in the trek fee: we help you book a cab from the Trekkaro hotel in Leh to the airport, paid directly to the driver.
If you have time to extend your stay, Ladakh has plenty more to see. Visit the historic Leh Palace, take in the panoramic views from the Shanti Stupa, or make a scenic trip to Pangong Lake. Try authentic Ladakhi cuisine before you leave and spend some time with the local culture that makes this region so distinct.
Whichever way you go, you leave having walked one of the most unusual trails in the Himalaya, on a river that is only a path for a short window each winter, from mid-January to mid-February.
What to Expect: Hotel check-out at 10:00 AM
Cab to Leh airport: not included; we help you book one, paid directly to the driver Optional extensions: Leh Palace, Shanti Stupa, Pangong Lake
Authentic Ladakhi cuisine before you fly out Trek ends at Leh
How To Reach
By Air
By Train
By Bus
Nearest airport: Kushok Bakula Rimpochee Airport (IXL), Leh, about 4 km from Leh town, with flights from Delhi and other major cities; international trekkers can fly into Delhi and connect to Leh. In winter flying is the only way to reach Leh, and January–February is peak Chadar season, so book your flights early.
From Leh Airport to the hotel:
airport transfers are not included in the trek fee; we help you book a cab from Leh Airport to the Trekkaro Leh Hotel, paid directly to the driver. You spend the first three days in Leh to acclimatise and complete the mandatory medical check; the drive from Leh to the trek start (Day 4) and back (Day 8) is included.
Return: On Day 9 we help you book a cab from the Trekkaro Leh Hotel to Leh Airport (airport transfers are not included in the trek fee; paid directly

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Sari
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Rishikesh → Sari (~185 km, 8–9 hrs) | Altitude: 340 m → 2,012 m (6,601 ft) | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay (triple or quad sharing)
Day 1 is a road day from Rishikesh (340 m) to Sari village, the base camp of the trek. Leave early, around 7:00 AM, and you reach Sari by evening without rushing. The 185 km drive takes 8 to 9 hours and follows the river valleys of Garhwal, past the sacred confluences at Devprayag and Rudraprayag and through the town of Srinagar.
Rudraprayag is the last reliable ATM before Sari. Withdraw enough cash there, as ATMs beyond it are unavailable or unreliable. After the river towns, the road climbs through Himalayan villages, green valleys and terraced fields.
Sari is a small, peaceful village and a good place to rest before the walking begins. You check into a homestay or guesthouse on a triple or quad sharing basis, and dinner is served there. Sari has a few small shops for basic trekking items, but we recommend you bring everything you need. Repack your daypack, drink plenty of water and sleep early.
What to Expect: Early start from Rishikesh, around 7:00 AM
185 km drive (8–9 hrs) via Devprayag, Srinagar and Rudraprayag
Last reliable ATM at Rudraprayag
Terraced fields and traditional Garhwali villages on the climb to Sari
Homestay or guesthouse at the base camp, dinner included Overnight: Sari (2,012 m / 6,601 ft)

itinerary.title: Sari to Deoriatal
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,012 m → 2,390 m (7,841 ft) | Distance: 3 km | Duration: 2–3 hrs | Terrain: gradual forest trail through oak, rhododendron and maple | Stay: Tents about 200 m from Deoriatal
Day 2 is the shortest and easiest walk of the trek, a gentle way in. You cover 3 km in 2 to 3 hours and gain about 378 m (1,240 ft). The trail climbs gradually out of Sari into thick forest of oak, rhododendron and maple. The gradient never turns hard. Use today to find your walking rhythm and to check that your boots and backpack sit right.
The forest is alive with the songs of Himalayan birds, which makes this stretch a favourite with birdwatchers and photographers. Walk quietly and you hear more. As you gain height, the trees open now and then and the first snow-clad peaks appear in the distance.
Then you reach Deoriatal at 2,390 m (7,841 ft). The lake sits in a ring of forest, and on a clear day its still water holds a sharp reflection of the Chaukhamba massif: the real range above and its mirror image below. Deoriatal also holds a place in local mythology and folklore, which gives it a quiet, spiritual feel.
Camp is set about 200 m from the lake. You arrive early, with lunch and evening snacks served at camp, so the afternoon is yours. Walk down to the lake, sit by the water and watch the light change on the peaks. Drinking water at camp is boiled or treated with chlorine tablets; check with your trek leader before you refill anywhere else. On a clear night the stars reflect on the lake. Put on warm layers before sunset.
What to Expect: Short, gradual 3 km climb with about 378 m (1,240 ft) of height gain Oak, rhododendron and maple forest full of birdsong Deoriatal Lake and its reflection of the Chaukhamba massif on clear days Free afternoon at the lake, with lunch and evening snacks at camp Stargazing over the water on clear nights Overnight: Tents about 200 m from Deoriatal (2,390 m / 7,841 ft)

itinerary.title: Deoriatal to Baniyakund via Rohini Bugyal
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,390 m → 2,610 m (8,562 ft) | Distance: ~16 km | Duration: 7–8 hrs | Terrain: gentle ascents, then rolling forest ridges with steep descents, alpine meadow | Stay: Tents at Baniyakund
Day 3 is the longest day of the trek, nearly 16 km over 7 to 8 hours. The net gain is only about 220 m (722 ft), but that number hides the work. The trail starts with gentle ascents, then turns into rolling terrain with steep descents that test your endurance. Start early, keep your breaks short and regular, and eat and drink a little at each one. On long rolling days, steady pacing matters more than speed.
Much of the day runs through the dense oak, maple and rhododendron forest of the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary. The air is fresh and the forest is full of birds. Keep an eye out for the Himalayan Monal, the colourful state bird of Uttarakhand; with luck, you spot one. As you gain height, the Chaukhamba massif and Mount Kedar rise behind the trees, and they stay with you through the day.
The trail then opens onto Rohini Bugyal, a wide alpine meadow and one of the highlights of the trek. In spring, red and pink rhododendrons bloom around it. In winter, it lies under snow. Take a proper break here and refuel, because forest ridges still lie between you and camp.
From Rohini Bugyal, the trail follows those ridges and small clearings, then descends gently to Baniyakund at 2,610 m (8,562 ft). The campsite is a wide, open meadow with snow peaks behind it. Watch the sun dip behind the summits, eat a good dinner and get to bed early. Tomorrow you climb to Tungnath and Chandrashila.
What to Expect: Longest day of the trek: nearly 16 km, 7–8 hrs Rolling forest terrain with gentle ascents and steep descents Oak, maple and rhododendron forest of the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary
Views of the Chaukhamba massif and Mount Kedar, and a chance of seeing the Himalayan Monal
Rohini Bugyal meadow, with rhododendrons in spring and snow in winter Overnight: Tents at Baniyakund (2,6

itinerary.title: Summit Day - Chopta to Tungnath and Chandrashila, back to Baniyakund
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Baniyakund → Chopta (short drive) | Altitude: 2,679 m → Tungnath 3,680 m → Chandrashila 3,962 m (13,000 ft) | Distance: 11 km | Duration: 8–9 hrs | Terrain: forest and meadow climb, steep final 1 km | Stay: Tents at Baniyakund
Summit day takes you to the Tungnath Temple and the top of Chandrashila. You leave Baniyakund early for the short drive to Chopta at 2,679 m (8,790 ft), a place known as the Mini Switzerland of Uttarakhand. This is the starting point of the walk to Tungnath.
The trail from Chopta climbs gradually through rhododendron and oak forest, then opens into wide alpine meadows with the Himalaya behind them. In spring the rhododendrons are in bloom; in winter the slopes are white with snow. The climb is long and steady rather than steep, so settle into a pace you can hold for hours. You reach Tungnath at 3,680 m (12,073 ft), the highest temple of Lord Shiva and one of the Panch Kedar shrines. The ancient stone temple stands against the mountains, and it is worth a quiet pause before the last climb.
From Tungnath, Chandrashila is only 1 km away, but this is the hard section of the day. The gradient is steep and the altitude is high, which makes the ascent moderately challenging. Take short steps, keep your breathing steady and pause briefly but often. In snow, plant your poles and walk in the line your guide sets. At 3,962 m (13,000 ft), the summit gives you a 360 view of snow-clad peaks: Chaukhamba, Kedarnath, Trishul, Bandarpoonch and Nanda Devi.
After time at the top, you retrace your steps to Tungnath, descend to Chopta and return to camp at Baniyakund. Take the steep upper section slowly on the way down. Back at camp, a hot dinner ends the biggest day of the trek.
What to Expect: Early start and short drive from Baniyakund to Chopta (2,679 m)
Steady climb through rhododendron and oak forest and open meadows Tungnath Temple (3,680 m / 12,073 ft), the highest temple of Lord Shiva
Steep final 1 km from Tungnath to Chandrashila

itinerary.title: Baniyakund to Rishikesh
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Baniyakund → Rishikesh (~200 km, 8–9 hrs) | Altitude: 2,610 m (8,562 ft) → 340 m The last day is a drive of about 200 km from Baniyakund down to Rishikesh, which takes 8 to 9 hours. You leave the crisp alpine air behind and follow the great rivers of Garhwal down the valleys, winding past sacred confluences and old mountain towns until the hills flatten out into the plains.
It is a good day to sit back and let the trek settle: the lake at Deoriatal, the long forest day to Baniyakund and the view from Chandrashila.
Meals on the road are not included, so keep some cash for a roadside stop. If you have onward travel booked, leave a margin for road delays. We recommend a late-evening or next-day departure from Rishikesh rather than a tight connection.
What to Expect: Drive of about 200 km from Baniyakund to Rishikesh, 8–9 hrs Road along the rivers of Garhwal, past sacred confluences and mountain towns Meals on the road are not included Keep a margin for road delays before onward travel Arrival in Rishikesh at the edge of the plains Trek ends at Rishikesh

From Rishikesh to Sari: The 185 km drive takes 8–9 hrs. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs (about ₹6,500 one way per 5–6 seat vehicle), paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers. The cab leaves Jumping Heights, Tapovan (Rishikesh) at 07:00 AM.
Return: The trek ends at Baniyakund; the cab leaves at 06:30 AM and reaches Jumping Heights, Tapovan by about 05:00 PM (200 km, 8–9 hrs; about ₹6,500 one way per vehicle, shared). Book your flight for the next day.
Nearest railway station: Haridwar Junction, about 25 km (around 1 hr) from Rishikesh, is the better-connected choice, with t

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Raithal
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Dehradun → Raithal (~180 km, 8–9 hrs) | Altitude: 2,256 m (7,400 ft) | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay (triple or quad sharing)
Day 1 is a road day. Start from Dehradun early, around 7:30 AM, so you reach Raithal by evening without delays. The 180 km drive takes 8 to 9 hours through the Garhwal Himalaya, past pine forests, small hill towns and the terraced fields of Uttarakhand.
Bhatwari, about an hour before Raithal, is the last reliable ATM and the last place with a stable mobile signal. Withdraw enough cash there, finish your important calls and tell your family you will be out of reach. After Bhatwari the signal is weak to non-existent, at Raithal and through the trek.
Raithal is a Himalayan village in Uttarkashi district and the base camp of the trek, with views of snow-clad peaks and warm local hospitality. You check into a guesthouse or homestay on a triple or quad sharing basis, and dinner is served there. The village has a few small shops for basic trekking items, but we recommend you carry everything you need. Sleep early tonight.
What to Expect: Early start from Dehradun, around 7:30 AM
180 km drive (8–9 hrs) past pine forests, hill towns and terraced fields Last ATM and last stable mobile network at Bhatwari, about 1 hour before Raithal
Village stay at Raithal with dinner included Only basic shops in Raithal, so bring what you need Overnight: Raithal (2,256 m / 7,400 ft)

itinerary.title: Raithal to Gui
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,256 m → 2,936 m (9,630 ft) | Distance: 5 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Terrain: village trail, then oak, pine and rhododendron forest | Stay: Tents at Gui
Day 2 is a short climb that sets you up for the summit. After breakfast at Raithal, the trail starts with a gradual ascent along village paths and then enters dense forest of oak, pine and rhododendron. You gain about 680 m (2,230 ft) over 5 km in 3 to 4 hours. The gradient is steady rather than steep, an easy-moderate walk that suits beginners. Go slowly in the first hour while your body adjusts to the height.
The forest is shaded and quiet, with the smell of pine and the rustle of leaves around you. As you climb, small clearings open in the trees and give you your first look at the snow-capped peaks in the distance. In spring and summer the forest fills with wildflowers and rhododendron blooms. In winter the trail carries a coat of snow, so take shorter steps and use your poles.
Gui, at 2,936 m (9,630 ft), is a campsite surrounded by alpine meadows and backed by high peaks, one of the most scenic overnight halts on this trek. You arrive with the afternoon ahead of you. Lunch and evening snacks are served at camp. Rest, keep drinking water and take a short walk around the meadow instead of spending the whole afternoon in the tent.
As the sun sets, the snow summits turn orange and gold. After a warm dinner, step outside. On a clear night the sky over Gui is full of stars, and it is a good spot for night photography. Then sleep early. Tomorrow starts at sunrise.
What to Expect: Gradual 5 km climb with about 680 m (2,230 ft) of height gain Shaded oak, pine and rhododendron forest First views of snow peaks from clearings in the forest Snow on the trail in winter; wildflowers and rhododendrons in spring and summer Sunset on the peaks and a clear night sky for stargazing Overnight: Tents at Gui (2,936 m / 9,630 ft)

itinerary.title: Summit Day - Gui to Dayara Top and back to Gui
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,936 m → 3,749 m (12,300 ft) → 2,936 m | Distance: 10 km (round trip) | Duration: 8–9 hrs | Terrain: oak, maple and rhododendron forest, open meadow, steep snowy slopes near the top | Stay: Tents at Gui
Summit day is the most challenging and most rewarding day of the Dayara Bugyal Trek. After an early breakfast, you start at sunrise. The trail passes the meadows near Gui and enters a dense forest of oak, maple and rhododendron. The first stretch is a gradual climb. Then comes a steeper ascent of about half an hour towards Chilapada, the first real test of your stamina. Slow down, shorten your stride and keep your breathing even. In winter the forest floor is sprinkled with snow and catches the morning light.
Out of the forest, the trail opens onto Dayara Bugyal, one of the largest high-altitude pastures in India. In spring and summer it is green grass and wildflowers. In winter it turns into a wide white carpet of snow. The walk across the meadow is rolling and open, and the Garhwal Himalaya fills the skyline: Bandarpoonch, Black Peak, Mt Srikanth, Draupadi ka Danda, Mt Jaunli and Bakariya Top.
The final stretch to Dayara Top is a steeper climb across undulating snowy slopes. This is the hard section. Step into the footprints ahead of you, plant your poles and take short pauses rather than long stops. Put on microspikes if your trek leader asks you to. At 3,749 m (12,300 ft), the top gives you a 360 view of the Garhwal Himalaya, with snowfields running into peaks on every side. You spend some time here and have light refreshments before you turn around.
The return follows the same route, back across the bugyal and down through the forest. The descent takes less effort, but snow and a cold breeze still demand care. The sunset lights up the peaks on the way down, and you reach Gui by late evening. Dinner is hot and sleep comes quickly.
What to Expect: Sunrise start after an early breakfast Steep half-hour climb towards Chilapada through oak,

itinerary.title: Gui to Raithal, drive to Dehradun
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,936 m → 2,256 m (7,400 ft) | Distance: 5 km | Duration: 2–3 hrs | Drive: Raithal → Dehradun (180 km, 8–9 hrs) | Stay: Not included The last day starts with breakfast at Gui and an easy walk down. You retrace the familiar forest trail through oak, maple and rhododendron, and the downhill is far gentler than the climbs of the last two days. The 5 km to Raithal take 2 to 3 hours. Through the trees you catch glimpses of terraced farms and the Garhwal peaks in the distance.
At Raithal, the base camp, there is time for a short break and a chat with the villagers before the long drive back.
Then you set off on the 180 km road journey to Dehradun, 8 to 9 hours of winding mountain roads, valleys and river crossings. Breakfast is the only meal included today, so plan for lunch on the road. The cab reaches Dehradun Railway Station by about 09:00 PM.
What to Expect: Easy 5 km descent to Raithal, 2–3 hrs Glimpses of terraced farms and the Garhwal peaks from the forest trail Short break in Raithal village before the drive 180 km drive to Dehradun, 8–9 hrs Breakfast is the only meal included today Trek ends at Raithal; drop at Dehradun Railway Station by about 09:00 PM

Nearest airport: Jolly Grant Airport (DED), about 25 km and 45–60 min from Dehradun city, with direct flights from Delhi and other metros. The cab to Raithal leaves Dehradun Railway Station at 07:30 AM, so fly in the day before and stay the night in Dehradun.
From Dehradun to Raithal:
The 180 km drive takes 8–9 hrs. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs (about ₹6,500 one way per 5–6 seat vehicle), paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers. The cab leaves Dehradun Railway Station at 07:30 AM.
Return: On the last day the cab leaves Raithal at around 01:00 PM and reaches Dehradun Railway Station by about 09:00 PM (about ₹6,500 per vehicle, shared). Book your flight for the next day.

itinerary.title: Drive from Dehradun to Agoda
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Dehradun → Agoda (185 km, 8–9 hrs) | Altitude: 640 m → 2,250 m (7,382 ft) | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay at Agoda
Day 1 is a long road day, so it starts early. We recommend reaching Dehradun Railway Station a little before the 7:30 AM departure, so the drive can begin on time and you reach Agoda before dark. The road climbs into the Himalayas through valleys, pine-clad slopes and busy hill towns, then enters the quieter Uttarkashi district.
For most of the day you follow the Bhagirathi River upstream, through Uttarkashi and then Sangamchatti, before the road turns into the Assi Ganga Valley. Uttarkashi is the last reliable ATM before Agoda, so withdraw the cash you need there. Meals on the drive are not included.
By evening you reach Agoda, at 2,250 m, a small village surrounded by forests and terraced fields and the starting point of the trek. You stay in a guesthouse or homestay on a triple or quad sharing basis, and dinner is served here. Agoda is the last place with a stable mobile signal, and only Jio works consistently, so make your calls tonight.
What to Expect: Long drive from Dehradun to Agoda: 185 km, 8–9 hrs Road along the Bhagirathi River through Uttarkashi and Sangamchatti
First views of the Assi Ganga Valley as you near the trailhead Last reliable ATM at Uttarkashi; at Agoda only Jio works consistently Dinner at the guesthouse or homestay, triple or quad sharing Overnight: Guesthouse / homestay at Agoda (2,250 m / 7,382 ft)

itinerary.title: Agoda to Manjhi
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,250 m → 2,700 m (8,860 ft) | Distance: about 10 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: gradual forest trail through oak, deodar and rhododendron, with open meadows | Stay: Tents at Manjhi
Day 2 is your first walking day, and it is a gentle one. You leave Agoda after breakfast, and the trail climbs gradually into thick forest of oak, deodar and rhododendron. The canopy keeps you in shade for long stretches, and gaps in the trees give you glimpses of the surrounding valleys. The gradient stays easy all the way, and there is no hurry: the walk is about 10 km, and you reach camp by afternoon with time to rest. Find a pace you can hold for an hour without stopping, and let your breathing settle into it.
The forest is the best part of today. Birdsong follows you most of the way, and now and then you hear a mountain stream running near the trail. The section between Agoda and Manjhi is one of the best on the trek for spotting Himalayan birds and langurs, and for photographs of sunlight falling through the trees, so keep your camera within reach. Between the forest sections the trail crosses stretches of open meadow. Pause at these. They give you the first views of the snow-clad ridges.
You reach Manjhi by early afternoon. It is a small settlement of scattered shepherd huts set among lush grasslands, and the campsite sits beside a clear stream. You sleep in tents on a triple sharing basis, with a large mess tent for meals. At 2,700 m, Manjhi is a good acclimatisation stop before you go higher. In our experience the short day lets your body adjust without strain.
After lunch the afternoon is yours. Walk out across the meadows, sit by the water, or simply rest and enjoy the stillness. Tea, coffee, soup and snacks are served regularly at camp. Mobile signal is unavailable once you leave Agoda, so tonight is a quiet first night in tents.
What to Expect: First trekking day: about 10 km, 5–6 hrs, a gradual climb from Agoda
Shaded forest of oak, deodar and rh

itinerary.title: Manjhi to Dodital Lake
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,700 m → 3,050 m (10,006 ft) | Distance: 5 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Terrain: gentle, steady climb through rhododendron, oak and pine forest | Stay: Tents by Dodital Lake
After a warm breakfast at Manjhi, you walk back into the forest. The trail keeps climbing gently under a dense canopy of rhododendron, oak and pine. The distance is short, only 5 km, but the steady climb makes it a 4–5 hour walk, so keep the same slow, even pace as yesterday. Clear streams run along the trail, and alpine flowers grow at its edges.
This is a quiet, shaded stretch. Shafts of sunlight come down through the trees, the air is crisp in the shade, and the sound of the streams stays with you as you climb. In spring the rhododendrons bloom and the trail turns red and pink. Then, late in the walk, the forest opens up all at once and Dodital Lake is in front of you.
Dodital sits at 3,050 m. It is a clear, emerald freshwater lake surrounded by meadows, with snow-dusted peaks behind it. Locally it is also called Dhundi-tal or Ganesha-ka-tal, and it is sacred: it is believed to be the birthplace of Lord Ganesha. A small Ganesh Temple stands on the bank, and trekkers stop there for blessings. The lake feeds the Assi Ganga River, which later joins the Bhagirathi at Gangori. In winter the lake partially freezes and the forest around it lies under thick snow.
Camp is pitched by the lake, in tents on a triple sharing basis, and this is your home for the next two nights. Spend the evening strolling the lakeside meadows and watch trout swim in the clear water. Evenings at Dodital get chilly even in summer, when nights on this trek drop to 0–7 C, so put on a light woollen or down jacket before the sun goes down. Use the evening to sort your daypack for the long climb to Darwa tomorrow.
What to Expect: Gentle 5 km climb through rhododendron, oak and pine forest Clear streams and alpine flowers along the trail; rhododendrons in bloom in spring First view of Dodital Lake as the for

itinerary.title: Summit Day - Dodital to Darwa Pass and Darwa Top, back to Dodital
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,050 m → 4,150 m (13,615 ft) → 3,050 m | Distance: 10 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: steep birch and rhododendron forest, alpine meadows, rocky ridges | Stay: Tents by Dodital Lake
Today is the most demanding day of the trek, and the most rewarding. You eat an early breakfast by the lake and set out for Darwa Top at 4,150 m. The climb is steep at times. The trail first runs through birch and rhododendron forest, then the trees thin out into alpine meadows. Lunch is packed today, so carry it along with plenty of water and snacks. The extension to Darwa is a real step up from the walk to the lake, and we recommend it for trekkers with good fitness and some prior experience.
Above the meadows the ascent becomes rugged. The trail crosses rocky ridges and narrow passages, and this is the hard section of the day. Shorten your steps, place your feet with care, and stop to catch your breath rather than pushing through. The trekkers who climb slowly here have the most energy left for the final push. As the trees fall away behind you, the views of the snow-capped ranges grow wider with every ridge you gain.
The final push takes you to Darwa Pass and then on to Darwa Top. From the top you get a full 360 panorama of the Garhwal Himalaya. Bandarpunch (6,316 m) and Swargarohini (6,252 m) stand out, with Kala Nag and Draupadi ka Danda among the peaks around them. On a clear day the view extends all the way toward the Gangotri range. Spend time here, take photographs and eat your packed snacks before you start down.
You return to Dodital by the same trail, reaching camp by late afternoon or evening. The descent feels gentler and gives you time to look around: alpine flowers, marmots, or even Himalayan griffons flying overhead. Walking poles are very useful on the steep sections going down. Back at the lake, the same camp and a hot dinner are waiting for you.
What to Expect: Early start for the hardest day: 10 km, 6–7 hrs, out and back from Dodital
Steep

itinerary.title: Dodital to Agoda
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,050 m → 2,250 m (7,382 ft) | Distance: 15 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: long descent on the forest trail, meadows and river crossings | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay at Agoda
Today you walk all the way down from Dodital to Agoda. It is the longest walking day of the trek, 15 km and 6–7 hours, but the descent is comfortable. After breakfast you leave the lake and head down into the forest. Going down is faster, but we recommend taking your time. Start with your warm layers on, as the morning by the lake is cold, and take them off once you warm up in the forest.
The steeper forest stretches are where your knees take the strain. Trekking poles are a blessing today. Use them on every steep drop, let them take some of your weight on each step down, take small steps and keep your knees soft rather than locked. The forest is rich in birdlife on the way down, and if you walk quietly you may spot woodpeckers, barbets or Himalayan magpies.
Lower down, the trail makes its river crossings and passes Manjhi and its shepherd huts once more. You stop for lunch near Manjhi, then continue downhill through forest and meadow on the last stretch to Agoda. Keep sipping water through the day. It is easy to forget on a descent, and a long downhill day still tires you out.
You end the day back in Agoda, where a guesthouse or homestay waits on a triple or quad sharing basis. After the nights in tents, a bed and a roof feel especially good, and the warmth of the village is a welcome change. Agoda also brings back mobile signal, though only Jio works consistently. Eat a good dinner and rest your legs. If they feel sore, a slow walk around the village in the evening helps more than sitting still. Tomorrow is a long day on the road.
What to Expect: Longest walking day: 15 km, 6–7 hrs, all downhill from Dodital
Long forest descent, with woodpeckers, barbets and Himalayan magpies possible River crossings and the shepherd huts of Manjhi on the way down Lunch near Manjh

itinerary.title: Drive from Agoda to Dehradun
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Agoda → Dehradun (185 km, 8–9 hrs) | Altitude: 2,250 m → 640 m (2,100 ft) | Stay: Not included (trip ends on arrival at Dehradun)
Your last morning starts early in Agoda. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs, paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers, and the cab leaves Agoda at around 07:00 AM for Dehradun Railway Station. The drive is 185 km and takes 8–9 hours, retracing the mountain roads you came up on.
The road follows the Assi Ganga down to Sangamchatti and then joins the Bhagirathi River, so you stay close to Himalayan rivers nearly the whole way. You pass through Uttarkashi, a busy Himalayan town, and get your last views of the Garhwal ranges before the road drops to the plains. Meals on the drive are not included, so plan to buy food on the way.
The cab reaches Dehradun Railway Station by about 06:00 PM. Your stay in Dehradun is not included. We recommend booking your train or flight home for late evening or the next morning, which leaves buffer time in case the drive runs long.
What to Expect: Early departure from Agoda, around 07:00 AM
Shared cab to Dehradun Railway Station, not included in the trek fee Drive along the Assi Ganga and Bhagirathi rivers through Uttarkashi
Last views of the Garhwal ranges before the plains Book onward travel for late evening or the next morning Trek ends at Agoda; drop at Dehradun Railway Station by about 06:00 PM

From Dehradun to Agoda: The 185 km drive takes 8–9 hrs. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs (about ₹6,500 one way per 5–6 seat vehicle), paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers. The cab leaves Dehra

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Gangotri
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Pickup: Dehradun Railway Station, 6:30 AM | Drive: Dehradun → Gangotri (3,065 m / 10,056 ft) | Activity: Temple visit, gear check, health baseline, acclimatisation walk | Overnight: Gangotri
The drive to Gangotri is an approach that earns its own place in the experience. From Dehradun, the road climbs through Mussoorie and Dharasu before joining the Bhagirathi River at Uttarkashi. From Uttarkashi onwards, the road follows the Bhagirathi upstream through a gorge that narrows and deepens progressively as altitude increases, the river visible far below in stretches of churning white water between sheer canyon walls of granite and schist. The scale of the valley tightens around the road as you climb. By the time Gangotri appears, a cluster of stone buildings and temple structures in a high valley at 3,065 metres, the contrast between the narrow gorge behind you and the relative openness of the Gangotri basin provides an immediate and visceral sense of arrival.
Gangotri is one of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites, the four sacred destinations of Hindu tradition. The Gangotri Temple, dedicated to the goddess Ganga, sits at the bank of the Bhagirathi River and has been a site of religious significance for centuries. The town itself exists at the intersection of two worlds: the pilgrimage world of the Char Dham circuit and the mountaineering world that uses Gangotri as the base for expeditions to Shivling, Meru, Bhagirathi, and the surrounding peaks. This duality of devotion and mountaineering, ancient tradition and modern adventure, gives Gangotri a character unlike any other trek gateway in India.
The afternoon is structured for acclimatisation, gear check, and preparation. Trekkaro's health baseline is taken at Gangotri: SpO₂, pulse, and blood pressure for every trekker, recorded as the individual reference point for all subsequent daily readings. The trek briefing covers the route, daily structure, health monitoring protocol, AMS awareness specific to the al

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Chirbasa
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,065 m (10,056 ft) → 3,600 m (11,808 ft) | Distance: ~9 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Terrain: Forest trail, riverside gorge path, rocky sections above treeline The trail from Gangotri to Chirbasa follows the right bank of the Bhagirathi River upstream through the Bhagirathi gorge, one of the most dramatically enclosed and geologically exposed valley walks in the entire Himalayan range. The gorge walls above the trail are vertical in sections, composed of ancient granite, gneiss, and schist in layered formations that display hundreds of millions of years of geological history in visible cross-section. The river below is fast, white, and extraordinarily loud in the early sections where the gorge is at its narrowest, a sound so constant and so powerful that it becomes a kind of baseline noise that shapes the entire character of the day's walk.
The trail through the gorge passes through birch and pine forest in the lower sections before the treeline retreats and the terrain opens to bare rock and alpine scrub. Chirbasa – 'place of the chir pine' in the local dialect – sits at the point where the last significant tree cover ends, at 3,600 metres. The campsite is positioned on a rocky shelf above the river with the first clear views of the Gangotri peaks: the Bhagirathi massif is visible from Chirbasa, its glacially carved ridgelines rising above the upper valley in a sequence that previews the scale of what lies ahead. The Gangotri Glacier itself is not yet visible from Chirbasa, but the landscape has already become one that the lower valley, for all its drama, did not contain.
Day 2 is a sustained but manageable introduction to the route; the altitude gain of approximately 1,800 feet over 9 km is within the range most prepared trekkers handle comfortably. Use the day to establish your rhythm on the gorge path, to begin adapting to the reduced oxygen at Chirbasa's altitude, and to observe the geological and ecological changes that occur across the 9

itinerary.title: Chirbasa to Bhojbasa
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,600 m (11,808 ft) → 3,775 m (12,385 ft) | Distance: ~5 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Terrain: Open rocky valley, lateral moraine, last section above treeline The trail from Chirbasa to Bhojbasa is shorter in distance than the previous day but no less significant in what it reveals. The gorge walls that enclosed the lower route open gradually as altitude increases, and the valley floor, previously narrow and forested, widens into a broad, open glacial valley that frames the upper mountain terrain on all sides. The Gangotri Glacier, one of the longest glaciers in the Garhwal Himalayas at approximately 30 kilometres, becomes visible in the middle section of this day's walk as the lateral moraine of its lower terminus appears on the right side of the valley. The scale of the glacier, even seen from a lateral distance, is immediately and genuinely astonishing. This is not a small alpine snowfield. This is a river of ice that has carved the valley you are walking through over geological time.
Bhojbasa, named for the birch (bhoj) trees that are the last surviving vegetation at this altitude, sits at 3,775 metres in a flat, open section of the valley with the full span of the Gangotri Glacier visible in the distance and the Bhagirathi group of peaks rising above it. Bhagirathi I (6,856 m), Bhagirathi II (6,512 m), and Bhagirathi III (6,454 m) form a spectacular vertical wall of rock and ice on the valley's eastern side that is visible in full from the Bhojbasa campsite. Shivling, still partially obscured by the valley ridgeline at this point, shows its upper reaches, enough to understand what is coming tomorrow.
Bhojbasa is the acclimatisation camp before the Gaumukh day. The altitude here, 3,775 m / 12,385 ft, is a significant step above Chirbasa and requires a rest afternoon rather than further exertion. Eat a full dinner, drink 3 litres minimum, and be in your sleeping bag by 9:00 PM. The evening health check at Bhojbasa is among the most important

itinerary.title: Bhojbasa to Gaumukh & Ascent to Tapovan
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,775 m (12,385 ft) → Gaumukh (3,892 m / 12,770 ft) → Tapovan (4,463 m / 14,640 ft) | Distance: ~9 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs | Terrain: Valley trail to glacier, glacier moraine crossing, steep ascent to Tapovan meadow Day 4 is the physical and emotional centrepiece of the Gaumukh Tapovan trek and one of the most memorable single trekking days in the accessible Indian Himalayas. The day begins with the walk from Bhojbasa to Gaumukh, approximately 4 kilometres along the valley floor, with the Gangotri Glacier growing in scale and proximity with every step. The glacier snout at Gaumukh sits at 3,892 metres, and the approach to it requires walking across the loose, unstable terrain of boulders and glacial debris that demands careful foot placement and the use of trekking poles as constant anchors. Your trek leader guides every trekker through the moraine crossing individually, assessing line choices in real time.
Gaumukh itself, the terminal face of the Gangotri Glacier from which the Bhagirathi River emerges as a white torrent from beneath the ice, is an experience that resists adequate description. The scale of the ice is the first thing: walls of grey-white glacial ice three to five storeys high, fractured and fissured and groaning with the slow movement of 30 kilometres of accumulated ice pressing from above. The sound is constant, the roar of the river emerging beneath, the occasional crack of ice fracture, and the movement of meltwater in channels across the glacier surface. And beneath all of it, the knowledge of what this place is: the source of the sacred Ganga, the origin point of a river that has defined civilisation in northern India for millennia. Most trekkers stand at Gaumukh for longer than they planned to. The ice, the river, the scale, and the significance of the place combine in a way that is genuinely difficult to move away from.
