itinerary.title: Tapovan to Bhojbasa
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 4,463 m (14,640 ft) → 3,775 m (12,385 ft) | Distance: ~9 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: Moraine descent from Tapovan, glacier crossing, valley trail to Bhojbasa
The morning of Day 5 begins with the final dawn at Tapovan. One night at the high meadow, watching Shivling catch the first light is an experience that compresses days of trekking into a single, defining image. Be outside before first light one last time. The mountain deserves a proper farewell. After breakfast, the descent begins.
The descent from Tapovan to Gaumukh reverses the Day 4 ascent: down the moraine from the meadow edge, across the loose boulder terrain above the glacier snout, past Gaumukh for a second view of the ice face, and then along the valley trail back toward Bhojbasa. The descent covers approximately 9 km and takes 5 to 6 hours, with the moraine section requiring the same careful attention as the ascent. At altitude, descents are physically harder on the knees than the climb; the eccentric load on the quad muscles through the moraine sections demands deliberate foot placement and the constant use of trekking poles for shock absorption.
Bhojbasa at 3,775 m feels different on the return: warmer than Tapovan, with the reappearance of vegetation and the sound of the Bhagirathi River reasserting the familiar acoustic landscape of the lower valley. Dinner at Bhojbasa on Day 5 is a different kind of meal from the meals at Tapovan, the relief of lower altitude, the sense of having done what you came to do, and the knowledge that Gangotri is now only one day away, all contributing to an atmosphere at the Bhojbasa camp on the return that is warmer and more expansive than the focused, demanding nights of the ascent.
What to Expect: Dawn at Tapovan: be outside 45 minutes before sunrise for one final view of Shivling in first light Moraine descent from Tapovan: careful foot placement required – same terrain as ascent, technically demanding going down Second view of Gaumukh

itinerary.title: Bhojbasa to Gangotri
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,775 m (12,385 ft) → Gangotri (3,065 m / 10,056 ft) | Distance: ~14 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: Gorge trail along the Bhagirathi River — Bhojbasa to Chirbasa to Gangotri
The final trekking day of the Gaumukh Tapovan circuit reverses the approach route from Bhojbasa to Chirbasa to Gangotri – 14 kilometres along the Bhagirathi gorge, with altitude falling steadily from 12,385 feet to 10,056 feet over 5 to 6 hours. The gorge trail on the return is the same trail you walked on Days 2 and 3, but the body walking it is different. Five days at altitude, one night at 14,640 feet, a glacier crossing, and a Tapovan dawn have accumulated into a physical and psychological state that perceives the return route differently from the approach.
The reappearance of the forest, birch first at Chirbasa, then pine, progressively denser as altitude falls, is one of the more affecting transitions of the return. Above Chirbasa, the landscape is bare rock, glacier, and sky. Below Chirbasa, life returns in increments: the first scrubby alpine plants, then the birch trees, then the sound of birds in the lower forest. By the time you reach Gangotri, you are back in a world that contains trees and buildings and the specific smell of a sacred river town incense, pine smoke, temple flowers, and the ever-present roar of the Bhagirathi below the temple steps.
The trek officially concludes at Gangotri. Trekkaro issues completion certificates at the assembly point. The valley that brought you here in anticipation now returns you with experience, the specific, unrepeatable, permanent experience of having stood at the source of the Ganga and slept one night in a meadow beneath Shivling at 14,640 feet. The drive to Dehradun begins from Gangotri tomorrow. Tonight, rest in the temple town at the foot of the Bhagirathi gorge.
What to Expect: Final trekking day: 14 km from Bhojbasa to Gangotri through the Bhagirathi gorge Forest returns: birch at Chirbasa, then pine, then the

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Dehradun
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 3,065 m (10,056 ft) → Dehradun (~640 m) | Distance: ~241 km by road | Duration: ~10–11 hrs drive | Departure: Gangotri → Uttarkashi → Dharasu → Dehradun
The final day of the Gaumukh-Tapovan trek is the drive from Gangotri back to Dehradun, approximately 241 km through the Bhagirathi Valley and out to the plains. The road descends through Uttarkashi, Chinyalisaur, and Dharasu and down through the Doon Valley to Dehradun, reversing the approach journey. Where the drive in was charged with anticipation, the drive out carries a different weight: the accumulated experience of seven days, one glacier crossing, one high-altitude camp, and a dawn beneath Shivling.
The Bhagirathi gorge, encountered in full on the drive out, is the same geological drama that bordered the trek on Days 2 and 6, the same vertical canyon walls, the same roaring river far below, and the same sequence of narrowing and widening as the road descends. From a vehicle window, the scale of what you trekked through becomes newly visible. The gorge that took two days to walk in takes a few hours to drive. The body knows what the car does not.
The trek officially concluded yesterday at Gangotri. Today's drive is the final chapter, Gangotri to Dehradun, the Bhagirathi Valley to the Doon Valley, and mountain air to the plains. The journey that brought you here in anticipation now takes you back with experience, the specific, unrepeatable, permanent experience of having stood at the source of the Ganga and slept one night in a meadow beneath Shivling at 14,640 feet. The valley looks different going out. It is the same valley. You are different.
What to Expect: Drive day: Gangotri to Dehradun – ~241 km, ~10–11 hours through the Bhagirathi Valley
The gorge on the drive: the Bhagirathi gorge visible from the road – the same valley that enclosed the trek Altitude drops ~2,400 m from 3,065 m at Gangotri down to Dehradun in the Doon Valley – lungs fully restored Gangotri Temple: departure fr

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Hanuman Chatti
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Pickup: Dehradun Railway Station, 6:30 AM | Drive: Dehradun → Hanuman Chatti (162 km, 7–8 hrs) | Altitude: 2,134 m (7,000 ft) | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay (triple or quad sharing)
Day 1 is a road day. The cab leaves Dehradun Railway Station at 6:30 AM, and you reach Hanuman Chatti before dark. The 162 km take 7 to 8 hours. The road climbs through Mussoorie, then runs via Damta, Naugaon, Barkot and Syana Chatti, with deep valleys, pine and oak forest, and the Yamuna alongside.
Barkot, about 1 hour 30 minutes before the base camp, is the last reliable ATM and the last stable mobile network; Jio does not work well in this region. Withdraw enough cash and finish your calls there. Shops higher up mostly take cash, and the signal is almost gone by Hanuman Chatti.
Hanuman Chatti is a peaceful village in Uttarkashi district and the base camp for the trek. It lies on the road to Janki Chatti, which is 5 km from the Yamunotri Temple. You stay in a guesthouse or homestay on a triple or quad sharing basis, with dinner included. Spend a quiet evening by the river and sleep early.
What to Expect: Early start from Dehradun Railway Station at 6:30 AM
162 km drive (7–8 hrs) via Mussoorie, Barkot and Syana Chatti
Last ATM and stable mobile network at Barkot
Yamuna River views and pine and oak forest along the road Quiet evening by the river, dinner included Overnight: Hanuman Chatti (2,134 m / 7,000 ft)

itinerary.title: Hanuman Chatti to Kandola
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,134 m → 2,590 m (8,500 ft) | Distance: 5 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Terrain: gradual forest trail of pine, oak and maple, past Nishni village | Stay: Tents at Kandola
Day 2 begins with a light breakfast and a short briefing from the Trekkaro team, and you set off at 7:00 AM. The walk to Kandola is a gradual ascent of about 456 m (1,500 ft) over 5 km, which takes 3 to 4 hours. It is a gentle first day and a good one for finding your rhythm.
Soon after Hanuman Chatti, the trail enters dense forest. Tall pine, oak and maple trees close overhead, and the path is covered with fallen brown maple and pine leaves, soft and quiet underfoot. The only sounds are birdsong and rustling leaves. Walk at a pace where you can still talk. If you are too out of breath to speak, slow down.
Partway up, you pass through Nishni village, a small hamlet of traditional wooden houses and terraced farms. The climb is mild around the village, and it is a good place for a short break and a look at mountain life up close.
The last stretch brings you to Kandola at 2,590 m (8,500 ft). The campsite sits among forest and mountain slopes, with views of the surrounding ridges. Lunch and evening snacks are served at camp, and the afternoon is yours to rest. Drinking water at camp is boiled or treated with chlorine tablets; ask your trek leader before you refill anywhere else. At sunset the sky over the ridges glows warm, and on a clear night the stars are out in full. Sleep early. Tomorrow is the longest day of the trek.
What to Expect: 7:00 AM start after breakfast and a short briefing Gradual 5 km climb with about 456 m (1,500 ft) of height gain Dense pine, oak and maple forest on a leaf-covered trail Nishni village, with wooden houses and terraced farms Sunset and sunrise views over the ridges from camp Overnight: Tents at Kandola (2,590 m / 8,500 ft)

itinerary.title: Summit Day - Kandola to Gulabikantha via Seema Thatch and back
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,590 m → 3,200 m (Seema Thatch) → 3,658 m (12,000 ft) → 2,590 m | Distance: 14 km (7 km up, 7 km down) | Duration: 7–8 hrs | Terrain: pine and oak forest, alpine meadow, steeper climb to the summit | Stay: Tents at Kandola
Summit day is long, so you start early from Kandola with a packed lunch in your bag. The first part of the trail winds through dense pine and oak forest at a steady gradient, which gives you time to warm up before the real climbing. The forest then opens onto the alpine meadows of Seema Thatch at 3,200 m (10,500 ft), with rolling hills around you and wildflowers in season. Take a short break here and drink water.
Above Seema Thatch the trail turns steeper. This is the hard section of the day, and it stays with you until the top. The full ascent takes about 4 to 5 hours. Climb in short steps, pause briefly and often, and keep your breathing steady. In winter, snow adds to the effort, so use your poles and walk in the line your guide sets.
At the Gulabikantha summit, 3,658 m (12,000 ft), the view opens in a full 360 circle. Peaks line the skyline: Bandarpoonch, Black Peak, Swargarohini, Kalindi Srikala, Chaukhamba, Draupadi ka Danda and Jorkanden, along with the Shivalik mountains. Clouds drift across the ridges. You eat your packed lunch at the top, take your photographs and rest.
Then you retrace your steps down through Seema Thatch to Kandola. The return is quicker, but it is still 7 km downhill on tired legs, so keep your poles out and your steps short. The evening at camp is relaxed. Dinner, a warm tent and a starlit sky over the forest close the day.
What to Expect: Early start with a packed lunch for the summit Pine and oak forest, then the meadows of Seema Thatch (3,200 m / 10,500 ft)
Steeper climb above Seema Thatch; about 4–5 hrs of ascent in total 360 summit view including Bandarpoonch, Swargarohini, Black Peak and Chaukhamba
Lunch at the summit, then descent by the same route Overnight: Tents at Kandola (2,590 m

itinerary.title: Kandola to Hanuman Chatti
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,590 m → 2,134 m (7,000 ft) | Distance: 5 km | Duration: 2–3 hrs | Terrain: steady downhill through pine and oak forest, some steep patches | Stay: Guesthouse / homestay at Hanuman Chatti
The last walking day is short and easy. You have breakfast around 7:00 AM and start down from Kandola. The trail is a steady descent of about 456 m (1,500 ft) over 5 km, back through the pine and oak forest you climbed through on Day 2. It takes 2 to 3 hours.
Easy does not mean careless. There are some steep descending patches, and trekking poles make a real difference on them. Keep your weight over your feet, shorten your stride on the steep parts and let the poles take load off your knees. On the way you pass Nishni village again, and the trees open to views over the Yamuna Valley.
The trek concludes at Hanuman Chatti. If you want more from the day, Garam Kund, a natural hot water spring, is a short 3 km away by road or on foot. We recommend the dip. The warm, mineral-rich water is believed to soothe sore muscles after summit day.
You spend the night at a guesthouse or homestay in Hanuman Chatti on a triple or quad sharing basis, with lunch and dinner included. Take a slow walk through the village lanes in the evening. The locals are warm, and a few words in their language are always appreciated.
What to Expect: Breakfast around 7:00 AM, then an easy 5 km descent Some steep patches on the way down; trekking poles help Nishni village and views over the Yamuna Valley
Optional 3 km trip to the Garam Kund hot spring Evening walk through the village lanes Overnight: Hanuman Chatti (2,134 m / 7,000 ft)

itinerary.title: Hanuman Chatti to Dehradun
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Hanuman Chatti → Dehradun (162 km, 7–8 hrs) | Altitude: 2,134 m (7,000 ft) | Route: Syana Chatti, Barkot, Naugaon, Damta, Mussoorie
The last day is the drive back to Dehradun, about 162 km and 7 to 8 hours by road. The route runs through Syana Chatti, Barkot, Naugaon and Damta, then descends via Mussoorie into the Doon Valley. Pine and oak forest line the road, and the Yamuna flows alongside in parts.
Barkot is the first place on the way down with a reliable ATM and mobile network, and a good spot for a short halt. Meals on the road are not included, so plan a stop for lunch.
As the road winds down, the cool mountain air gives way to the plains. You arrive in Dehradun by evening, with easy onward connections by train, bus or flight.
What to Expect: 162 km drive, 7–8 hrs, via Barkot, Naugaon, Damta and Mussoorie
Yamuna River and pine and oak forest along the road ATM and mobile network again at Barkot
Meals on the road are not included Evening arrival with onward train, bus and flight connections Trek ends at Hanuman Chatti; drop at Dehradun Railway Station by evening How To Reach
By Air
By Train
By Bus
Nearest airport: Jolly Grant Airport (DED), about 25 km and 45–60 min from Dehradun city, with direct flights from Delhi and other metros. The drive to Hanuman Chatti takes 7–8 hrs, so fly in the day before and stay the night in Dehradun.
From Dehradun to Hanuman Chatti:
The 162 km drive takes 7–8 hrs. Transport is not included in the trek fee: we help the group book shared cabs (about ₹6,500 one way per 5–6 seat vehicle), paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers. The pickup is at Dehradun Railway Station at 06:30 AM on Day 1.
Return: On the last day we help the group book a shared cab from Hanuman Chatti to Dehradun (not included in the trek fee; about ₹6,500 one way per vehicle, paid directly to the driver and split among trekkers); the drive takes 7–8 hrs. Book your flight for the next day.
Nearest railway station: Dehradun Railway

itinerary.title: Manali to Jobra & Trek to Chika
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Manali → Jobra (~23 km, ~45 min) | Trek: Jobra → Chika | Distance: ~2 km | Duration: 1-2 hours | Altitude: 9,800 ft → 10,400 ft The Hampta Pass trek begins not with a dramatic vertical climb but with one of the gentlest, most beautiful introductions in Himalayan trekking. From Jobra, a quiet forest clearing near the Hampta village above Manali, the trail enters a dense cover of oak, birch, and conifer that filters the morning light into slanted gold columns. The Hampta stream runs alongside the path, visible through the trees and audible even when obscured, its glacial chill adding a particular quality of freshness to air that is already noticeably colder and cleaner than anything you breathed in Manali. This is the Himalayas at their most welcoming: physically unhurried, visually generous, and immediately removed from the noise of the world below.
The first day's trail is a confidence builder by design. The elevation gain is modest, roughly 600 feet over 2 kilometres, and the terrain is a well-defined forest path with some rocky sections near the stream crossings. First-time trekkers find their rhythm here, learning how their body responds to uphill movement at altitude and settling into the pace their guide sets. More experienced trekkers use the day to assess their kit: checking whether their boots are broken in enough, calibrating their layering to the ambient temperature, and adjusting their pack so that the weight sits correctly on their hips rather than their shoulders.
After approximately 1.5 hours of steady walking, the forest opens suddenly and dramatically into the wide, flat meadow at Chika. The transition from enclosed forest to open alpine meadow is one of the recurring visual rewards of the Hampta Pass trail, and it first delivers itself here in a way that stops most trekkers mid-step. Chika sits in a glacially carved valley bowl at 10,400 feet, ringed by green ridges and snow-patched peaks. The meadow is wide enough that tents s

itinerary.title: Chika to Balu Ka Ghera
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 10,400 ft → 12,200 ft | Distance: ~8.5 km | Duration: 6 hours | Terrain: Alpine meadows, river crossings, moraine Day 2 is when the Hampta Pass trail reveals itself in earnest. The gentle forest introduction of Day 1 gives way to a wide, open valley that climbs steadily toward the base of the pass in a series of terraced meadows separated by stream crossings and moraine fields. From the moment you leave Chika, the scale of the surrounding terrain becomes apparent in a way that the forest canopy had partially obscured. The ridgelines are higher. The peaks are closer. The valley ahead narrows visibly in the distance, converging on the snowy V-shaped notch of the pass itself, still a day away but already visible as a distinct feature on the horizon.
The trail to Balu Ka Ghera passes through some of the most spectacular open meadow terrain on the entire route. The Hampta River, which at this elevation is more accurately described as a collection of braided glacial streams flowing together across a wide, flat valley floor, provides a series of crossings that require careful foot placement and occasionally wet boots, depending on the time of season and the day's snowmelt rate. In June and early July, these crossings can be knee-deep and fast-moving; by August and September, they are ankle-deep and manageable with trekking poles for balance. Your guide will assess each crossing and assist trekkers individually if the water level is significant.
The upper section of the day's trail passes through a boulder field and low moraine before arriving at Balu Ka Ghera, literally 'home of sand' in the local dialect, named for the alluvial deposits that characterise the campsite's terrain. At 12,200 feet, Balu Ka Ghera is positioned directly at the foot of the pass approach, and the view from camp looking up the valley is one of the most memorable on the trek. The glacial headwall that forms the upper valley is fully visible, streaked with snow even in peak s

itinerary.title: Balu Ka Ghera to Hampta Pass & Descent to Shea Goru
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 12,200 ft → 14,100 ft → 11,800 ft | Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 7-8 hours | Terrain: Snow, scree, steep ascent and descent This is the day the entire trek has been building toward, and it earns its reputation completely. The Hampta Pass crossing is the defining experience of the trek – the physical, emotional, and visual centrepiece around which everything else organises itself. It is a demanding day: 10 kilometres of total distance, close to 2,000 feet of altitude gain in the morning followed by a steep 2,300-foot descent in the afternoon, all at elevations between 12,000 and 14,100 feet, where the available oxygen is roughly 40% less than at sea level. It is also the most scenic day of walking on this trek.
Departure from Balu Ka Ghera is early, 5:30 AM to 6:00 AM – to take advantage of the morning's firmer snow and to ensure the group crosses the pass and completes the descent before afternoon weather builds. The first two hours are a sustained ascent up the glacially carved valley above camp. The terrain is a mix of compacted snowfields, loose scree beneath the snow, and occasional exposed rock sections where the trail becomes a steep scramble. Your trek leader moves at a measured pace that prioritises consistent forward movement over speed. The altitude demands deliberate breathing; many trekkers adopt a rhythmic step-breath pattern that becomes almost meditative over the course of the ascent. Fixed ropes are installed by the Trekkaro technical team on the steepest section just below the pass, a safety measure that converts a potentially dangerous exposed slope into a confidently manageable climb.
The pass itself is a narrow, rocky ridge at 14,100 feet. When you step onto it, the world divides. Behind you: the green, water-rich Kullu Valley; the forested ridges of Manali visible in the far distance; and the braided streams of the Hampta River glittering two thousand feet below. In front of you: the Lahaul-Spiti Valley, grey and silver

itinerary.title: Shea Goru to Chhatru and Drive to Chandratal Lake & back
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Trek: Shea Goru → Chhatru | Distance: ~6 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Altitude: 11,800 ft → 10,900 ft | Drive: Chhatru → Batal → Chandratal Lake ( 60 km, ~2 hrs) | Walk to lake: ~2 km | Return to Chhatru overnight After the enormous physical and emotional investment of Day 3, the morning of Day 4 begins gently and unhurriedly. The 6-kilometre trail from Shea Goru to Chhatru follows the Chandra River along the floor of the Lahaul Valley – mostly flat, occasionally undulating, with the river in constant sight and the dramatic bare ridgelines of the Spiti ranges flanking both sides of the path. This is the Himalayas with all softness removed: wide, open, and elemental, lit by a hard directional light that falls on bare rock with no canopy to diffuse it. Formations of deep rust, pale ochre, silver-grey, and dark volcanic brown rise above the path in layered geological exposures that read like pages of a very long book. You are walking across the floor of an ancient inland sea, and the landscape makes that legible in ways that no geology lesson could.
The Chandra River is one of the significant rivers of the western Himalayas, the headwater of the Chenab, and walking alongside it at this elevation carries a particular weight of significance. The river runs glacial-blue and fast, fed by snowfields above that are still visible on the ridgelines. Many trekkers use this morning to process what happened the previous day: the pass, the descent, the landscape change, the fixed rope, and the moment on the ridge looking both ways. The mountains have given you something significant, and the easy morning walk gives you time to sit with it before the afternoon's second extraordinary experience begins. Chhatru is reached in three to four hours, a remote settlement at the junction of the Manali-Kaza Highway and the Hampta Valley trail, sitting at the confluence of the Chandra River and the road into Spiti. After a hot lunch at camp, the Trekkaro vehicles load up, and the af

itinerary.title: Chhatru to Manali via Atal Tunnel
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Chhatru → Atal Tunnel → Manali | Distance: ~65 km by road | Duration: ~3–4 hours | Altitude: 10,900 ft → 6,700 ft The final morning at Chhatru arrives with the particular quality of light that belongs only to high-altitude Lahaul: flat, clean, and hard-edged, falling across the grey river gravel and bare ridgelines without any warmth of forest or meadow to soften it. You have slept two nights now on the Spiti side of the Hampta Pass, and the landscape has done its work on you. There is a specific kind of quiet that belongs to this terrain – wider and more absolute than the quiet of the forested Kullu Valley – and the final morning at Chhatru is when most trekkers sit with it most consciously, knowing it will not be available on the other side of the mountain. Breakfast is taken at camp as the team packs the last of the equipment and the vehicles are loaded. Then the drive begins.
The route from Chhatru to Manali follows the Chandra River westward before entering the Rohtang La area and descending through the Atal Tunnel – the 9.02-kilometre tunnel that bores straight through the Rohtang Pass mountain at 10,171 feet and emerges on the Kullu Valley side near Solang Valley. Named after former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, the Atal Tunnel is an engineering landmark of considerable scale – it is the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet – and it transforms a journey that once required crossing the dangerous Rohtang Pass road into a direct, year-round connection between Lahaul and Manali. The tunnel entrance on the Lahaul side sits in the bare, treeless terrain that has been your world for two days. The tunnel exit on the Manali side opens into a pine forest. The contrast – from grey rock and open sky to green, fragrant forest in the space of fifteen minutes – is so sudden and so complete that it feels almost theatrical. You step out of the mountain and back into the valley you started from.
The descent from the tunnel to Manali fol

itinerary.title: Drive from Dehradun to Sankri
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Dehradun → Mussoorie → Purola → Mori → Sankri | Distance: ~200 km | Duration: 8–9 hrs | Altitude: 640 m (Dehradun) → 1,950 m (Sankri)
The drive from Dehradun to Sankri is one of the longer approach journeys in the Trekkaro portfolio, approximately 200 km and 8 to 9 hours, through some of the most scenic and progressively remote terrain in Uttarakhand. The road passes through Mussoorie (2,000 m) before descending into the Yamuna and then Tonnes River valleys, following roads that become narrower and quieter as they penetrate deeper into the Garhwal interior. The Tonnes Valley carries the Tonnes River, the largest tributary of the Yamuna by volume, through a landscape of forested ridges, terraced fields, and small market towns. The drive is a genuine introduction to the region you are entering.
Sankri (1,950 m) is the departure point for several significant Uttarakhand treks, including Kedarkantha and Har Ki Dun. It is a small, well-organised trek gateway with the Swargarohini range visible above the village on clear days. The evening in Sankri is for rest, gear verification, and the trek briefing. Trekkaro's health baseline SpO₂, pulse, and blood pressure for every trekker is recorded here. The trek briefing covers the full route, daily structure, health monitoring protocol, and what to expect on the Supin Valley forest terrain. Sleep well. Day 2 begins early.
What to Expect: Drive from Dehradun to Sankri – ~200 km, 8–9 hrs via Mussoorie, Purola, and the Tonnes Valley road Tonnes Valley scenery: forested ridges, terraced farms, and progressively remote Garhwal interior Sankri (1,950 m): established trek gateway with Swargarohini views on clear days Free Trekking Gear: Decathlon trekking shoes, jacket, trekking poles, gaiters and microspikes Health baseline: SpO₂, pulse, and BP recorded for every trekker Trek briefing: full route overview, daily structure, health protocol Overnight: Sankri (1,950 m) – last road town before the trek begins

itinerary.title: Drive Sankri to Taluka & Trek to Puani Garaat
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Sankri → Taluka (~12 km, ~45 min) | Trek: Taluka (2,107 m) → Puani Garaat (~2,440 m) | Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 6–7 hrs Day 2 begins with the short morning drive from Sankri to Taluka, the last motorable point on the Har Ki Dun approach road. Taluka (2,107 m) is a small settlement at the point where the jeep track ends and the foot trail begins, marked by a bridge across the Supin River and the visible opening of the forested gorge ahead. From this bridge, on clear days, the snowpeaked wall at the head of the Har Ki Dun valley is visible as a distant white horizon above the forest canopy. You leave the road behind and begin the walk that will carry you up to 3,536 metres in three days.
The trail from Taluka to Puani Garaat follows the right bank of the Supin River upstream through a gorge of exceptional character. The Supin at this altitude is fast and loud, constrained between canyon walls that rise steeply on both sides. The forest above the trail is one of the ecological highlights of this route, with dense oak, deodar cedar, and rhododendron in the lower sections, giving way to blue pine and silver fir as altitude increases. In spring, the rhododendron bloom transforms the forest floor and canopy into layers of red and pink. In autumn, the oak and maple canopy turns amber and gold above a trail that remains dry and well-defined.
Puani Garaat is a forest camp in a clearing above the Supin River at approximately 2,440 m, a sheltered, well-watered campsite surrounded by forest and the sound of the river below. This is the first genuine wilderness camp of the route. Beyond Taluka, there are no roads, and the sounds of the trail are the river, the forest, and the wind. The altitude gain from Taluka is modest, approximately 330 m across 10 km, making Day 2 an ideal introduction to the terrain and the specific rhythm of Supin Valley trekking.
What to Expect: Morning drive from Sankri to Taluka (~12 km, ~45 min) - last road before the trail beg

itinerary.title: Puani Garaat to Kalkatiyadhaar
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: ~2,440 m → ~2,740 m (Kalkatiyadhaar) | Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 5–6 hrs | Terrain: Forest trail, river crossings, Osla village, open meadow approach Day 3 is the route's richest in cultural and ecological variety. The trail from Puani Garaat continues upstream along the Supin River, passing through the living village of Osla before climbing through progressively higher forest terrain to the meadow camp at Kalkatiyadhaar. Osla is one of the traditional villages of the Supin Valley, a settlement of stone and timber houses built in the distinctive Garhwali style with intricately carved wooden facades and stacked-stone construction that reflects centuries of craft adapted to the high-altitude climate. The village is genuinely inhabited and genuinely connected to an older version of Himalayan life.
In Osla stands the Duryodhana Temple, one of the most unusual religious sites in Uttarakhand and one of the very few temples in India dedicated to Duryodhana, the primary antagonist of the Mahabharata. The local tradition holds that the Pandavas passed through the Har Ki Dun valley on their ascent to heaven via the Swargarohini peak and that the Kauravas maintained a protective presence over the valley in their absence. The temple is small, stone-built, and decorated in the carved wooden style of the valley. Standing in Osla beside this temple, at the base of the Swargarohini massif, the mythological landscape of the Mahabharata and the physical landscape of the Himalayas briefly become the same thing.
Above Osla, the trail climbs through forest to Kalkatiyadhaar, a meadow camp at approximately 2,740 m where the forest gives way to the more open terrain of the upper Supin Valley. From Kalkatiyadhaar, the higher peaks of the Har Ki Dun enclosure become visible for the first time in their full extent: Swargarohini above and to the north, the Black Peak ridge to the east, and the valley corridor opening ahead toward the floor at 3,536 m. Tomorrow the

itinerary.title: Kalkatiyadhaar to Har Ki Dun Valley & Back to Kalkatiyadhaar
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: 2,740 m → Har Ki Dun (3,536 m / 11,600 ft) → Return to Kalkatiyadhaar (2,740 m) | Distance: ~14 km round trip | Duration: 8–9 hrs | Terrain: Open valley trail, alpine meadow Day 4 is the centrepiece of the Har Ki Dun trek, the day the entire route has been building toward. The trail from Kalkatiyadhaar to the Har Ki Dun valley floor gains 796 m over 7 km of progressively opening terrain. The forest thins above camp, the valley walls recede on both sides, and the landscape transforms from an enclosed forest gorge to a wide, open, high-altitude basin in a transition that happens gradually enough to absorb but dramatically enough to stop most trekkers mid-stride when the valley fully opens.
The Har Ki Dun valley at 3,536 m (11,600 ft) is an enclosed glacial basin of exceptional spaciousness. The valley floor is wide and flat in the summer and autumn seasons, a broad meadow of alpine grass and wildflowers crossed by the upper Supin River in clean, shallow channels that reflect the peaks above. On all three sides, the mountain wall rises: Swargarohini I (6,252 m) to the north-northwest, its upper snowfields brilliant white above the moraine at its base; Bandarpunch (6,316 m) directly north, its glacier visible as a grey-white river of ice between the rock ridges; and Black Peak (6,387 m) to the northeast. The 270-degree mountain panorama from the Har Ki Dun valley floor is among the most complete available on any moderate-grade trek in India. No pass crossing required. You simply walk into the valley and look up.
The return from the valley floor to Kalkatiyadhaar descends the same 796 m across 7 km in the afternoon. Most trekkers spend the middle of the day in the Har Ki Dun valley, time to walk the valley perimeter, photograph the mountain panorama from different positions, eat lunch at the riverbank, and be fully present with one of the finest valley views accessible on a moderate Himalayan trek. The afternoon light on the return illuminates th

itinerary.title: Kalkatiyadhaar to Puani Garaat
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Altitude: ~2,740 m → ~2,440 m (Puani Garaat) | Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Terrain: Forest descent, Supin Valley trail, Osla village on return Day 5 reverses the Day 3 ascent: from Kalkatiyadhaar back through the Supin Valley forest to Puani Garaat, passing through Osla and along the riverside trail that carried you upward two days ago. The descent covers 10 km and loses approximately 300 m of altitude across 4 to 5 hours, a gentle, unhurried return through terrain that has become familiar but that reveals itself differently on the way down.
The return through Osla on Day 5 produces a different experience from the Day 3 passage. Two days in the mountains have settled the group into the rhythm of the route. The urgency of the approach and the goal of reaching the valley ahead have been replaced by the fuller attention that comes after the destination has been reached. The Duryodhana Temple and the traditional wooden architecture of the village are absorbed with a different quality on the return. If time allows, the Trekkaro guide will arrange a brief stop in the village.
Puani Garaat, reached in the mid-afternoon, is the same forest camp as Night 2. But it feels different: warmer on the return and more settled. The Har Ki Dun valley is behind you. Taluka and the road are one day's walking ahead. The route has given you what it came with, and the forest camp on the final descent has a quality of completion that the camp on the ascent could not yet contain.
What to Expect: Descent through the Supin Valley forest – same trail as Day 3, reverse direction Osla village on return – Duryodhana Temple and traditional architecture, brief stop if schedule allows Distance: ~10 km | Duration: 4–5 hrs | Altitude loss: ~300 m Supin River alongside the trail throughout – the sound and pace of the descent are shaped by the water Puani Garaat camp (~2,440 m) – final wilderness camp before the return to Taluka and the road Overnight: Puani Garaat – last camp o

itinerary.title: Puani Garaat to Taluka & Drive to Sankri
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Trek: Puani Garaat (~2,440 m) → Taluka (2,107 m) | Distance: ~8 km | Duration: 3–4 hrs | Then: Drive Taluka → Sankri (~12 km, ~45 min)
The final morning on the trail begins in the Puani Garaat forest camp. The walk back to Taluka is the shortest of the active trekking days, 8 km descending from 2,440 m to 2,107 m over 3 to 4 hours. The trail through the lower Supin Valley gorge on the return carries the same dramatic canyon walls and river sound as the approach, but now the body walking it has walked 44 km through the Garhwal interior and stood in the Har Ki Dun valley at 3,536 m with the Swargarohini range on three sides. The same forest, the same river, the same trail sections — all perceived through a different set of accumulated experience.
The altitude drops steadily through the lower gorge, with the Supin growing louder as additional tributaries join it below the camp. By mid-morning, Taluka appears: the familiar stone buildings at the end of the jeep track, the bridge across the Supin, and the shared cabs waiting on the far bank. The drive back to Sankri takes approximately 45 minutes along the jeep track. Sankri is reached in the early afternoon: mobile signal returns, devices can be charged, and the first road-town comforts in five days are available. The trek is not yet over; Dehradun and the city return tomorrow, but the walk is done.
What to Expect: Final trail section: ~8 km from Puani Garaat to Taluka through the lower Supin gorge Altitude drops ~330 m from Puani Garaat to Taluka – steady, well-defined descent Taluka bridge – the trail ends where it began, at the Supin River crossing Drive from Taluka to Sankri (~12 km, ~45 min) by shared cab, paid directly to the driver Sankri: mobile signal, device charging, first road-town facilities after five days Trek concludes at the Sankri starting point of the trek. Completion certificates issued.
Overnight: Sankri (1,950 m) - final night before the Dehradun return drive

itinerary.title: Drive from Sankri to Dehradun
itinerary.description:
Route Details: Drive: Sankri (1,950 m) → Mori → Purola → Mussoorie → Dehradun | Distance: ~200 km | Duration: 8–9 hrs The morning in Sankri before the return drive has a different quality from the morning five days ago when the village was the assembly point for a trek that had not yet begun. Then, the Swargarohini range visible above the village was a destination. Now, the body and mind that looked up at those peaks have walked to 3,536 m beneath them, stood in the valley at their base, and returned through the Supin River forest over five days of walking. The mountains above Sankri look the same. Everything else is different.
The drive from Sankri to Dehradun retraces the approach road in reverse, back down the Tonnes Valley through Mori and Purola, then via Mussoorie and the Doon Valley. The 8- to 9-hour journey covers the same forested gorge road that the approach drive may have passed through in darkness or in anticipation. By the time Mussoorie appears above the Doon Valley, the transition from the mountain interior back to the city is nearly complete. The Har Ki Dun valley, the Duryodhana Temple, the Supin River gorge, and the mountain panorama from 11,600 feet are now part of the specific, permanent collection of experiences that the Himalayas are uniquely able to provide.
What to Expect: Morning in Sankri – final morning tea in the trek gateway village before the return drive Drive Sankri to Dehradun – ~200 km, 8–9 hrs via Mori, Purola, and Mussoorie
Tonnes Valley on return: the forested gorge road in daylight, the approach in reverse Same-day evening trains and night buses from Dehradun are achievable with early Sankri departure; book flights for the next day Recommended: one additional night in Dehradun before onwards travel if the schedule allows How To Reach
By Air
By Train
By Bus
Nearest airport: Jolly Grant Airport (DED), about 25 km and 45–60 min from Dehradun city, with direct flights from Delhi and other metros. The cab to Sankri leaves Dehradun Ra
